method: Lectio Edition (SDIT): a synthesis of the full translation tradition — John Dryden (1697) in the public domain, informed by the major modern renderings (Mandelbaum, Fitzgerald, Fagles, Ruden) as research and checked against the Latin. No copyrighted translation is reproduced; the rendering is original modern English. Reviewed for fidelity.
overview: The Lectio Edition carries the Aeneid into clear modern English, keeping Virgil’s gravity and momentum without Dryden’s 17th-century couplets. Built from Dryden’s public-domain verse and checked against the Latin, it aims to let a modern reader feel the cost of Aeneas’s duty as directly as Virgil’s first readers did.
introduction:
The Aeneid is Rome's national epic — the story of Aeneas, a Trojan refugee who carries his household gods out of a burning city to found the race that will become Rome. Beneath the wars and wanderings it is about duty, loss, and the terrible cost of empire. This is the Lectio Edition — Virgil in clear, living English, made to be read straight through.

Virgil's hero is defined by one word, pietas — devotion to gods, country, and family — which we render not as cold "piety" but as faithfulness, the thread that runs through the poem. The names keep their familiar Roman forms (Aeneas, Juno, Venus, Jupiter, Dido). The famous line sunt lacrimae rerum we keep close to its weight: "there are tears for the way of things." The rendering synthesizes the tradition — from Dryden through Mandelbaum, Fitzgerald, and Fagles — checked against the Latin; it copies none of them.

divergences.phrase: sunt lacrimae rerum et mentem mortalia tangunt
divergences.lectio: “there are tears for things, and mortal matters touch the heart”
divergences.note: One of the most famous and most ambiguous lines in Latin. ‘Lacrimae rerum’ can mean ‘tears for things,’ ‘tears in the nature of things,’ or ‘the world’s tears.’ Lectio takes the reading most scholars favour — grief for the world’s suffering — while this note flags the ambiguity.

divergences.lectio: “I sing of arms and of a man”
divergences.note: Virgil’s opening fuses the Iliad (arms, war) and the Odyssey (the man, wandering) in three words. Lectio keeps the plain order and the indefinite ‘a man’ — Aeneas enters as one man, not yet a legend.

Aeneas’s defining virtue. Latin pietas means devotion to gods, country, and family — not modern religious ‘piety.’ Lectio renders it as ‘duty’ so the modern reader feels what drives him, noting the original term.

divergences.phrase: quidquid id est, timeo Danaos et dona ferentis
divergences.older: “Trust not their presents, nor admit the horse” (Dryden)
divergences.lectio: “Whatever it is, I fear the Greeks even when they come bearing gifts”
divergences.note: Laocoön’s warning is the most quoted line in the poem. ‘Danaos’ is one of Homer’s words for the Greeks; ‘et dona ferentis’ means ‘even (those) bearing gifts.’ Lectio keeps the proverb close to its familiar English shape rather than Dryden’s paraphrase, since the line has become a saying in its own right.

divergences.older: “Great queen, what you command me to relate / Renews the sad remembrance of our fate” (Dryden)
divergences.lectio: “The grief you ask me to bring back to life, my queen, is beyond words”
divergences.note: ‘Infandum’ means literally ‘unspeakable, not to be spoken’ — a grief language cannot hold. Lectio leads with that weight (‘beyond words’) instead of smoothing it into Dryden’s couplet, because the whole book turns on a man forcing himself to speak the unspeakable.

divergences.phrase: iacet ingens litore truncus, avulsumque umeris caput et sine nomine corpus
divergences.older: “A headless carcass, and a nameless thing” (Dryden)
divergences.lectio: “Now he lies a huge trunk on the shore, the head torn from the shoulders, a corpse without a name”
divergences.note: Priam, lord of all Asia, ends as an unnamed body on a beach — a deliberate echo of Pompey’s headless corpse on the Egyptian shore, which Virgil’s first readers would have caught. Lectio keeps the stark, plain nouns (‘trunk,’ ‘corpse without a name’) rather than softening the horror of an anonymous death for a king.

divergences.older: “Reduc'd to grind the plates on which you feed” (Dryden)
divergences.lectio: “drive you to gnaw and devour your very tables”
divergences.note: Celaeno's curse. The Latin mensae means the flat bread-trenchers the Trojans use as plates, not crockery — the prophecy is fulfilled harmlessly in Book 7 when they eat the bread loaves under their food. Lectio keeps the literal ‘tables’ and the cannibal menace of ‘gnaw,’ since the dread is the point; the relief comes later.

divergences.older: “go, seek that mother earth / From which your ancestors derive their birth” (Dryden)
divergences.note: Apollo's oracle. Lectio keeps the riddling compression — ‘ancient mother,’ not ‘mother earth’ — because the whole drama of the book turns on the phrase being misread: Anchises hears Crete, but the god means Italy, the land of Dardanus. To over-explain the line is to spoil Virgil's trap.

divergences.phrase: hic pestis acerba mihi... genitorem... amitto
divergences.older: “My dear, dear father, spent with age, I lost” (Dryden)
divergences.lectio: “There I lost my father Anchises, the comfort of all my cares and griefs”
divergences.note: The death of Anchises closes the book on its quietest note — no battle, no monster, just a plain sentence. Lectio resists Dryden's repetition (‘dear, dear’) and lets the loss land flat and heavy, the way the Latin does: the heaviest blow of the voyage gets the fewest words.

divergences.older: "Forc'd by my fate, I leave your happy land" (Dryden)
divergences.lectio: “I do not sail for Italy of my own free will”
divergences.note: Aeneas’s whole defense turns on these four words — the hardest, coldest thing he says to Dido. ‘Non sponte’ means ‘not of my own choosing’: he is following Italy, not seeking it. Lectio keeps the bleak literal sense rather than Dryden’s softer paraphrase, because the cruelty of the line is that he offers her no comfort, only the fact of fate.

divergences.older: "Too like the sparkles of my former flame" (Dryden)
divergences.lectio: “I recognize the marks of the old flame”
divergences.note: Dido’s admission that she loves again. ‘Vestigia flammae’ — the traces, the footprints, the scar — of the old fire. The line is famous beyond the poem: Dante puts it in Italian in the mouth of Beatrice. Lectio keeps Virgil’s plain, terrible recognition rather than Dryden’s prettier ‘sparkles.’

divergences.phrase: exoriare aliquis nostris ex ossibus ultor
divergences.older: "Rise some avenger of our Libyan blood" (Dryden)
divergences.lectio: “rise, some avenger, out of my bones”
divergences.note: Dido’s dying curse, and the seed of the Punic Wars: the ‘avenger from her bones’ is Hannibal, whom Virgil’s first readers would have heard instantly. The Latin is a strange, broken construction — an unnamed ‘someone’ commanded into being out of a grave. Lectio keeps ‘out of my bones’ over Dryden’s smoother ‘our Libyan blood,’ because the horror is that the curse rises from her own corpse.

divergences.older: “one destin’d head alone / Shall perish, and for multitudes atone” (Dryden)
divergences.lectio: “There will be only one — one life lost out of all of them, one life given for the many”
divergences.note: Neptune's terrible bargain: safe passage bought with a single death. The Latin caput is literally ‘head,’ here ‘a life’; pro multis means ‘in exchange for the many.’ Lectio keeps the stark accounting of the line — one for all — and resists Dryden's churchly ‘atone,’ which loads a later theology onto it (though Virgil's first Christian readers heard exactly that echo).

divergences.phrase: Euryalus forma insignis viridique iuventa, / Nisus amore pio pueri
divergences.older: “Euryalus a boy of blooming years… / Nisus, for friendship to the youth renown’d” (Dryden)
divergences.lectio: “Euryalus in the first flower of his youth, the handsomest of them, and Nisus, who loved the boy with all his heart”
divergences.note: The first appearance of the two friends who return to die together in Book 9. Virgil calls Nisus's love amor pius — the same pietas, faithful devotion, that defines Aeneas himself. Lectio renders it as wholehearted love rather than Dryden's cooler ‘friendship,’ keeping the warmth and the weight of the bond without narrowing it; the word the poet chose is the word for his hero's central virtue.

divergences.phrase: adytis cum lubricus anguis ab imis / septem ingens gyros, septena volumina traxit
divergences.older: elaborated into ‘the sacred monster’ over many lines (Dryden)
divergences.lectio: “a great snake came gliding — seven huge coils of it, seven slow loops dragging across the ground… and then slid back down into the depths of the tomb and was gone”
divergences.note: The serpent at Anchises' tomb. Virgil leaves it deliberately undecided whether the snake is the genius loci, the spirit of the place, or an attendant of the dead — and Aeneas himself ‘could not say.’ Lectio keeps that open question rather than resolving the omen, because the not-knowing is the point: the line between a sacred sign and a chance creature is exactly where the scene lives.

divergences.phrase: facilis descensus Averno... hoc opus, hic labor est
divergences.older: “Smooth the descent, and easy is the way... In this the task and mighty labour lies” (Dryden)
divergences.lectio: “the way down to the underworld is easy... But to retrace your step, to climb back out to the air above — that is the labor, that is the task”
divergences.note: The most quoted lines of the book: anyone can fall; the hard thing is to come back. Lectio keeps the plain antithesis (easy down / hard up) and the doubled close ‘hoc opus, hic labor est,’ rather than Dryden’s smoothing, because the whole descent is built on that contrast.

divergences.phrase: tu regere imperio populos, Romane, memento... parcere subiectis et debellare superbos
divergences.older: “’tis thine alone, with awful sway, / To rule mankind... / To tame the proud, the fetter’d slave to free” (Dryden)
divergences.lectio: “You, Roman — your art is to rule the nations with your power... to spare the conquered, and to crush the proud”
divergences.note: Rome’s mission statement, and Virgil’s definition of empire. Others (Greeks, by implication) get the arts of bronze, oratory, astronomy; Rome’s ‘art’ is power tempered by mercy. Lectio keeps the hard final balance — ‘spare the conquered, crush the proud’ — the line Romans took as their creed, with its cost left undisguised.

divergences.phrase: sunt geminae Somni portae... altera candenti perfecta nitens elephanto
divergences.older: “Thro’ the gate of iv’ry, he dismiss’d / His valiant offspring” (Dryden)
divergences.lectio: Aeneas leaves the underworld through the gate of ivory — the gate of false dreams — kept plain and unexplained
divergences.note: Virgil sends his hero back to the living through the gate reserved for false dreams, not the gate of horn for true shades — an ancient puzzle no one has fully solved. Lectio renders the gates without smoothing or explaining the choice, leaving the famous ambiguity open exactly as the Latin leaves it.

books.label: Book I
books.title: The Storm, and Carthage
paragraphs: Arms, and the man, I sing — the man who, driven by fate, was first to flee the shores of Troy and come to Italy and its Lavinian coast. Hard was the road that battered him over sea and land, for Juno's relentless rage hounded him at every turn; and bitter were the wars he fought before he could found his city and carry his gods into Latium — the gods from whom the Latin people came, the Alban fathers, and the high walls of Rome.

Muse, tell me the causes. What wound to her divinity, what burning grievance, drove the queen of heaven to force a man so faithful, so devoted, through such a gauntlet of disaster — to hurl one trouble after another in his path? Can there really be such anger in the hearts of gods?

There was an ancient city, Carthage, a colony out of Tyre, facing Italy far across the water, opposite the mouth of the Tiber — a city rich in resources and fierce in the arts of war. They say Juno loved it above all places on earth, more even than Samos. Here she kept her armor; here she kept her chariot. And it was her fixed ambition, if fate would only allow it, that this city should one day rule the world.

But she had heard that a people descended from Trojan blood would someday rise up and tear down those Tyrian towers — that from them would come a nation broad in power and proud in war, born to bring ruin to Libya. So the Fates were spinning it. The daughter of Saturn feared this, and she had not forgotten the old war she had waged at Troy for the sake of her beloved Greeks. And there were older wounds too, griefs that still festered deep in her heart: the judgment of Paris and the insult to her beauty; the race she hated; the honors paid to Ganymede, stolen up to heaven. Inflamed by all of it together, she kept hurling the storm-tossed Trojans — the few the Greeks and merciless Achilles had left alive — across the whole expanse of the sea, far from Latium. Year after year they wandered, driven around every ocean by fate. So vast was the labor of founding the Roman race.
They were barely out of sight of Sicily, sails set, glad and cutting the salt foam with their bronze prows, when Juno — nursing the eternal wound beneath her heart — said to herself:

"So am I to give up, beaten? Am I unable to keep this Trojan king from reaching Italy? The Fates forbid me, do they? And yet Pallas Athena could burn the whole Greek fleet and drown the men in the sea — all because of the madness and crime of one man, Ajax, son of Oileus. She flung Jupiter's own lightning down from the clouds, scattered their ships, churned up the waters with the winds; and Ajax, his chest pierced and breathing flames, she snatched up in a whirlwind and impaled on a jagged rock. But I, who walk as queen of the gods, sister and wife of Jupiter — I have been waging war on this one nation for all these years. And after this, who will still pray to Juno, or lay an offering on my altar?"

Burning with these thoughts, the goddess came to Aeolia, the homeland of storms, a country teeming with raging winds. There, in a vast cavern, King Aeolus holds the struggling gales and the howling tempests under his command and keeps them chained in their prison. They snarl and roar against the bars, furious, and the whole mountain echoes back their rage. Aeolus sits high above them with his scepter, soothing their tempers and bridling their fury — for if he did not, they would tear sea and earth and the deep sky itself away with them through the empty air. Fearing exactly this, the all-powerful Father shut them away in their dark cave, piled mountains on top of them, and set over them a king bound by a fixed treaty: one who knew, on command, when to rein them in and when to give them their head. To this king Juno now came as a suppliant, and she said:

"Aeolus — the Father of gods and king of men gave you the power to calm the waves or rouse them with the wind. There is a people I hate sailing the Tyrrhenian Sea right now, carrying Troy and its beaten gods toward Italy. Throw all your force into the winds. Sink their ships, or break them apart and scatter their bodies across the water. I have fourteen nymphs of rare beauty in my service. The loveliest of them all, Deiopea, I will join to you in marriage and make her yours forever, so that for this service she may spend all her years with you and make you the father of beautiful children."

Aeolus answered: "My queen, it is yours only to decide what you want; my duty is simply to carry it out. Whatever small kingdom I hold, whatever scepter, whatever favor I have with Jupiter — all of it is your gift. You let me take my place at the feasts of the gods; you made me master of the storms."

He finished, and turned his spear and drove it into the hollow flank of the mountain. The winds, as if formed into a column, came pouring out through the breach and swept across the land in a hurricane. They fell on the sea, the East Wind and the South and the squall-bringing Southwest all together, heaving it up from its deepest floor and rolling huge waves toward the shore. Then came the shouts of the men, the shriek of the rigging. In an instant the clouds tore the sky and daylight from the eyes of the Trojans; black night sat down on the water. The heavens cracked with thunder, the air flashed with lightning, and everywhere death stared the men in the face. Aeneas felt his limbs go cold and weak. He groaned, and stretching both hands toward the stars he cried out: "Three times, four times luckier were the men who died in front of their fathers' eyes under the high walls of Troy! Diomedes — bravest of the Greeks — why couldn't I have fallen on the plains of Troy and poured out my life on your spear, where fierce Hector lies cut down by Achilles, where giant Sarpedon lies, where the river Simois rolls so many shields and helmets and brave bodies under its current!"

While he flung out these words, a screaming gust from the north slammed straight into his sail and lifted the waves to the sky. The oars snapped; the prow swung around and gave the ship's whole side to the waves, and a mountain of water came down on them in a sheer wall. Some hung on the crest; for others the trough yawned open and showed bare ground at the bottom, the sea boiling among the sand. The South Wind drove three ships onto hidden reefs — reefs the Italians call the Altars, a vast ridge just under the surface. Three more the East Wind hurled from open sea onto the shallows and the sandbars, a wretched sight, and walled them in with banks of sand. One ship, carrying the loyal Lycians and their captain Orontes, was struck before Aeneas's own eyes: a towering wave crashed down on the stern, pitched the helmsman headfirst overboard, and spun the ship three times in place before the whirlpool swallowed it down. Here and there a few men could be seen swimming in the huge swell, with weapons, planks, and Trojan treasure scattered across the waves. Now the storm took the sturdy ships of Ilioneus and brave Achates, of Abas and old Aletes; every hull sprang its seams and let the deadly water pour in through the cracks.

Meanwhile Neptune sensed that the sea had been thrown into uproar — felt the storm let loose and the still waters churned up from the very bottom. Deeply disturbed, he lifted his calm face above the surface and looked out across the deep. He saw the fleet of Aeneas scattered all over the water, the Trojans crushed beneath the waves and the falling sky. And he saw, clearly, the tricks and the malice of his sister Juno. He called the East Wind and the West to him and said: "What is this arrogance, born of what pride of birth? You winds — you dare to throw earth and sky into chaos and heave up these mountains of water without my leave? I'll — but first I had better calm these waves. Next time you won't get off so lightly. Now get out, and tell your king this: the rule of the sea and the cruel trident were never given to him — they fell to me by lot. He holds those monstrous rocks of yours, winds, the house you live in. Let Aeolus strut around in that hall of his and play king over a prison of locked-up winds." He spoke — and before he had finished he had calmed the swollen sea, scattered the gathered clouds, and brought back the sun. Cymothoe and Triton, heaving together, pushed the ships off the sharp rocks; the god himself lifted them with his trident, opened a path through the vast shoals, and smoothed the sea while his chariot skimmed lightly over the waves. It was like what happens when a great crowd breaks into riot — the mob runs wild, torches and stones fly, fury hands them weapons — and then, if they catch sight of a man whose goodness and service have earned him respect, they fall silent and stand still to listen, and his words master their hearts and cool their rage. Just so the whole roar of the sea fell quiet the moment Neptune looked out over it; and the Father of the waters, with the sky now clear above him, wheeled his horses and gave his willing chariot its head. Worn out, the Trojans made for the nearest land and turned toward the shores of Libya.

There is a place tucked into a long inlet, sheltered by an island whose flanks break the open sea and split the swell into a quiet harbor. On either side huge cliffs rise like twin towers against the sky, and beneath them the water lies safe and silent. Above stands a backdrop of shimmering forest, a grove of dark, overhanging trees; and under the brow of the facing cliff is a cave hung with fresh water and seats of natural rock — the home of nymphs. Here a tired ship needs no cable to hold her, no anchor to bite the ground. Aeneas put in here with the seven ships he had managed to gather out of the whole fleet. The Trojans, aching for dry land, climbed out and stretched their sea-soaked bodies on the sand.

First Achates struck a spark from flint, caught the fire in dry leaves, fed it kindling all around, and coaxed the flame to life out of the tinder. Then, sick of the sea as they were, they hauled out the grain they had salvaged and the tools for grinding it, and set about drying what the storm had spoiled and crushing it on the stones. Meanwhile Aeneas climbed a cliff to scan the whole sweep of the open sea, hoping to catch sight of Antheus driven before the wind, or the Phrygian galleys, or Capys, or the high stern of Caicus. There wasn't a single ship in view — but down on the shore he spotted three stags wandering, and behind them whole herds grazing along the valley in a long line. He stopped, snatched up the bow and the swift arrows that loyal Achates carried, and brought down the leaders first, their antlered heads held high, then scattered the rest with his shots, driving the whole herd in confusion through the green woods. He didn't stop until he had stretched seven huge carcasses on the ground, one for each ship. Then he made his way back to the harbor and divided the kill among all his men. After that he shared out the wine that good Acestes had loaded aboard, jar by jar, when they left the Sicilian shore, and with these words he eased their grieving hearts: "Friends — we are no strangers to hardship. You have suffered worse than this, and a god will put an end to this too. You have sailed right up to Scylla's raging cliffs and heard the rocks roar; you have faced down the Cyclops and his cave. Pull yourselves together and let go of this fear and grief. Someday, perhaps, even this will be something we look back on and enjoy remembering. Through all these trials, through so many dangers, we are headed for Latium, where the Fates promise us a home and a quiet rest — where it is destined that the kingdom of Troy will rise again. Hold on, and keep yourselves alive for the better days to come."

So he spoke. But sick with worry as he was, he forced the hope onto his face and crushed the anguish down deep in his heart. His men set to work on their prey, ready for the feast. They flayed the hides off the carcasses and laid the meat bare; some cut it into pieces, still quivering, and spitted it; others set bronze cauldrons on the beach and tended the fires. Then they brought back their strength with the food, sprawled on the grass, filling themselves with old wine and rich venison. When their hunger was satisfied and the tables cleared, they fell to talking — and the talk turned, with mingled hope and dread, to the friends they had lost, wondering whether the missing men were still alive or had met their end and were past hearing any call. Above all, Aeneas — devoted as he was — mourned in silence the loss of fierce Orontes, and Amycus, and the cruel fate of Lycus, and brave Gyas and brave Cloanthus.

And now it was over — when Jupiter, looking down from the height of heaven over the sail-flecked sea, the spread of land, the coasts and the wide nations, paused at the top of the sky and fixed his eyes on the kingdom of Libya. And as he stood there turning such cares over in his mind, Venus came to him, sadder than anyone had ever seen her, her bright eyes brimming with tears, and said:

"You who rule the affairs of gods and men with your eternal power, and terrify them with your thunderbolt — what could my Aeneas have done to you that was so terrible? What could the Trojans have done? They have suffered so many deaths already, and now, for the sake of Italy, the whole world is being shut against them. You promised me, surely — at some turn of the years the Romans would come from them, leaders restored from the blood of Troy, who would hold the sea and all the lands under their law. What has changed your mind, Father? That promise was the one thing that consoled me for the fall of Troy and all that ruin — I weighed one fate against the other. And now the same bad luck still hounds these men, beaten down as they are. Where will you let it end, great king? Antenor could slip out from the middle of the Greek army, sail safely up into the Adriatic, past the roaring source of the Timavus where it bursts through nine mouths to the sea, and found his city of Padua, give his Trojans a home, hang up his weapons, and settle at last in peace. But we — your own children, the ones you've promised a place in heaven — we lose our ships, every one of them, betrayed (it's unbelievable) for the anger of one goddess, and are kept far from the shores of Italy. Is this the reward for being faithful to you? Is this how you restore us to power?"
The Father of gods and men smiled at her — that smile that clears storms from the sky — kissed his daughter lightly, and answered:

"Spare your fear, Venus. The destiny of your people stands fixed; nothing will move it. You will see your city, the promised walls of Lavinium; and you will lift great-souled Aeneas all the way up to the stars. Nothing has changed my mind. And since this worry gnaws at you, I'll tell you more — I'll unroll the secret book of the Fates further. Your son will fight a great war in Italy, crush its proud peoples, and lay down laws and walls for his men, until the third summer has seen him reign in Latium and three winters have passed since he beat the Rutulians. Then the boy Ascanius — Iulus now, his new name — will reign for thirty long years, and move the seat of power from Lavinium to a new fortress, Alba Longa, which he will build with great labor. For three hundred years the kingdom will stand under the line of Hector's people, until a royal priestess, Ilia, pregnant by Mars, will give birth to twin sons. Then Romulus, in the tawny hide of the she-wolf that nursed him, will take up the line, found the walls of Mars, and call the people Romans after his own name. On these I set no limits of space or time — I have given them empire without end. Even harsh Juno, who now wears out sea and land and sky with her dread, will think better of it, and join me in cherishing the Romans, the masters of the world, the people of the toga. So it is decreed. An age will come, as the years roll on, when the house of Aeneas will subdue the very land of Achilles and Agamemnon, and rule conquered Greece. Then a Trojan Caesar will be born of that glorious line, a man whose empire will reach to the ocean and whose fame will reach the stars — Julius, a name handed down from great Iulus. One day you yourself will welcome him into heaven, weighed down with the spoils of the East, and he too will be invoked in prayers. Then the harsh centuries will soften; war will be laid aside. Faith and Vesta, and Romulus with his brother Remus, will lay down the law. The terrible iron gates of War will be shut and barred; and inside, monstrous Rage, perched on a heap of weapons, his hands chained behind him with a hundred bands of bronze, will roar in horror through his bloody mouth."

Then Jupiter sent Mercury, son of Maia, down from heaven, so that the land and the new fortress of Carthage would open their doors to the Trojans, and Dido — not yet knowing the will of fate — would not turn them away from her borders. Mercury flew down through the wide air on beating wings and quickly stood on the shores of Libya. He carried out his orders, and the Carthaginians, just as the god intended, laid their fierce tempers aside. The queen above all put on a mood of calm and goodwill toward the Trojans.

But Aeneas, devoted as ever, had lain awake all night turning many things over in his mind. As soon as the kindly light of dawn arrived, he resolved to go out and explore this new country — to find out what shore the wind had thrown him on, who lived there, men or wild beasts, since the land looked uncultivated — and to bring back a sure report to his men. He hid his ships in a cove under the hollow cliffs, screened by trees and overhanging shade, and set out with only Achates beside him, two broad-bladed spears in his hand. There in the depths of the forest his own mother met him, wearing the face and dress of a young girl, with a girl's weapons — a Spartan huntress, or like one of those Thracian women who outrun the swift rivers. She had a bow slung from her shoulder, ready, her hair loose to the wind, her knees bare, her flowing robe gathered up in a knot. "Tell me, you two," she called first, "have you seen one of my sisters wandering out here, with a quiver slung on, wrapped in a spotted lynx-skin — or chasing a wild boar with the hunt in full cry?"

So Venus spoke, and her son answered: "I've seen no sister of yours, and heard none — though I don't know what to call you. Young woman? Your face is nothing like a mortal's; your voice doesn't sound human. You must be a goddess — Apollo's sister, or one of the nymphs. Whoever you are, be kind to us; lighten our hardship, and tell us at last what sky we are under, what coast of the world we've washed up on. We're wandering here, strangers, driven by the wind and the huge waves. We don't know the people or the place. I'll see that many a sacrifice falls for you at the altar."

"I hardly deserve such honor," said Venus. "It's only the custom of these Tyrian girls to carry a quiver and lace high purple boots up the leg. What you see is a Carthaginian kingdom — Tyrians, the city of Dido — but the land around it belongs to Libya, a people unbeatable in war. Dido rules here. She came fleeing from Tyre, running from her own brother. It's a long story of wrong, with many turns, but I'll tell you the heart of it. Her husband was Sychaeus, the richest landholder in Phoenicia, and she loved him with all her heart — her father had given her to him as a girl, joined to him in her first marriage. But her brother Pygmalion held the throne of Tyre, a monster of cruelty beyond all other men. Madness came between them. Pygmalion, blind with greed for gold and caring nothing for his sister's love, ambushed Sychaeus at the altar and killed him in secret, in cold blood. For a long time he hid the crime and fed the heartsick wife with empty hopes and lies. But the ghost of her unburied husband came to her in her sleep, lifting up a face strangely pale, baring the pierced chest and the bloody altar, and laid the whole hidden crime of that house open before her. He told her to flee, to leave her homeland fast; and to help her on the journey, he showed her where an old treasure of silver and gold lay buried in the earth. Shaken, Dido gathered companions for her escape — everyone who hated the cruel tyrant or feared him bitterly. They seized some ships that happened to be ready, loaded them with the gold (so Pygmalion's hoard went to sea instead), and a woman led the flight. They came at last to the place where you'll see the great walls and the rising fortress of new Carthage now, and bought as much ground as a single bull's hide could enclose — which is why it's called Byrsa, 'the Hide.' But what about you? Where do you come from? Where are you headed?"

He answered her question with a deep sigh, the words dragged up from the bottom of his chest: "Goddess — if I went back to the very beginning and traced the whole record of our suffering, and if you had the time to hear it, evening would close the gates of heaven on the sea before I finished. We come from ancient Troy — if the name of Troy has ever reached your ears — and after wandering across every sea, a storm threw us here on the Libyan coast by chance. I am Aeneas, faithful Aeneas, who carries my household gods rescued from the enemy in my ships — a name known, once, above the clouds. I am seeking Italy, my homeland, and a line descended from Jupiter himself. I set out onto the Phrygian sea with twenty ships, my goddess mother showing me the way, following the path the Fates laid down. Barely seven are left, battered by the waves and the wind. And I myself wander these Libyan deserts, unknown and in need, driven out of Europe and out of Asia both." Venus could not bear to hear him grieve any further, and broke in:

"Whoever you are, I don't believe heaven hates you — not when you've reached a Carthaginian city still drawing breath. Just go on, and take yourself to the queen's door. I can tell you this: your friends and your fleet are safe, brought back to harbor by a shift of the wind — unless my parents taught me to read the birds for nothing. Look up there — twelve swans in a joyful line. A moment ago Jupiter's eagle, swooping out of the clear sky, was scattering them across the open air. Now you can see them strung out in formation again, either touching down or already looking down at the ground they've chosen, wheeling and clapping their wings, circling the sky in a chorus of song. Exactly so, your ships and your young men are either safe in port or running into harbor under full sail. Go on now — follow the road where it leads you."

She finished, and as she turned away her neck shone rose-bright; her hair breathed out the divine fragrance of ambrosia; her gown flowed all the way to her feet; and in the way she walked, the true goddess stood revealed. Aeneas knew his mother, and called after her as she fled: "You too — why are you so cruel? Why do you keep mocking your son with these disguises? Why can't I take your hand in mine, really hear your voice and answer it?" With that reproach he turned toward the city. But Venus wrapped the two of them in a thick veil of mist as they walked, a dark cloud poured around them, so that no one could see them, lay a hand on them, or stop them to ask why they had come. She herself rose into the air toward Paphos, glad to see her home again — her temple there, and the hundred altars warm with Sabaean incense and breathing the scent of fresh garlands.

Meanwhile the two of them pressed on along the path. Soon they were climbing the hill that looms over the city and looks down on the towers facing it. Aeneas marveled at the sheer scale of it — where huts had stood not long ago — marveled at the gates, the noise, the paved streets. The Tyrians were hard at work: some pushing up the walls and heaving stones up by hand to build the citadel; some marking out a site for a house and trenching it round. They were choosing magistrates and a senate and sacred laws; over here they were dredging out a harbor, over there laying the deep foundations of a theater, and cutting huge columns out of the cliffs to crown the stage that was to come. It was like bees in early summer, busy in the sun across a flowering meadow — leading out the grown young of the hive, or packing the cells tight with liquid honey until they bulged with sweet nectar, or taking in the loads brought home, or massing in a line to drive the lazy drones away from the hive. The work hums; the honey breathes of thyme. "How lucky you are," Aeneas said, gazing up at the rising rooftops, "you whose walls are already going up!" And, wrapped in cloud — astonishing to tell — he walked straight in among them, into the thick of the crowd, and no one saw him at all.

In the heart of the city there was a grove, deeply shaded and welcome, where the Carthaginians, fresh off the waves and the storm, had first dug into the ground and turned up the sign Juno had promised them: the head of a spirited horse, an omen that their people would be brave in war and rich in the years to come. Here Dido was building a vast temple to Juno, splendid with offerings and with the presence of the goddess herself. Its threshold rose on bronze steps; bronze held the beams together; the doors swung on hinges of groaning bronze. And it was here, in this grove, that something Aeneas saw for the first time eased his fear and let him dare to hope for better days. For while he waited for the queen, taking in the whole temple, wondering at the city's good fortune, at the skill of the rival craftsmen and the weight of their labor — he suddenly saw, painted across the walls in order, the battles of Troy, the war whose fame had already gone out over the whole world: the sons of Atreus, and Priam, and Achilles, savage to them both. He stopped, and the tears came. "Achates," he said, "is there any place left on earth that isn't full of what we suffered? Look — there's Priam! Even here, glory has its reward; there are tears for the way of things, and the troubles of mortal men touch the heart. Let go of your fear. This fame of ours will somehow keep us safe." He spoke, and fed his soul on the empty picture, sighing again and again, the tears running in rivers down his face. For he saw the fighting around Troy — here the Greeks in flight as the young Trojans pressed them, there the Trojans running with crested Achilles bearing down on them in his chariot. Not far off he wept to recognize the white-canopied tents of Rhesus, betrayed in their first sleep and ravaged by bloody Diomedes, who slaughtered the men and drove the fiery horses back to the Greek camp before they could taste the grass of Troy or drink from its river. Elsewhere he saw Troilus, just a boy, no match for Achilles, his weapons thrown away, in flight — fallen flat on his back, dragged behind his own empty chariot, still gripping the reins; his neck and his hair sweeping the dust, the dust scrawled over by the trailing point of his spear. Meanwhile the Trojan women were walking to the temple of Athena, who would not be appeased, their hair undone, carrying her a robe, beating their breasts in grief — and the goddess kept her eyes fixed on the ground, turned away. Three times Achilles had dragged Hector around the walls of Troy and was selling his lifeless body for gold; and Aeneas groaned aloud, deep from the heart, to see the spoils, the chariot, the very body of his friend, and Priam reaching out his old, defenseless hands. He recognized himself, too, in the thick of the Greek chiefs; and the columns out of the East, and the armor of black Memnon. There Penthesilea led her ranks of crescent-shielded Amazons, raging through the heart of the fighting, a golden belt cinched under her bare breast — a warrior queen, a girl who dared to meet men in battle.

And while Aeneas stood there marveling, fixed and lost in the sight of it all, queen Dido swept toward the temple in radiant beauty, a great throng of young men crowding around her. She was like Diana leading her dancing nymphs along the banks of the Eurotas or over the ridges of Cynthus — a thousand mountain spirits gathering behind her on every side, while she carries her quiver and walks a head taller than them all, and a silent joy stirs in the heart of her mother Latona. Just so was Dido; just so she moved, glad and serene, through the midst of her people, pressing on the work and the future of her kingdom. Then, at the door of the goddess, beneath the very center of the vaulted roof, she took her seat on a high throne, ringed by her guards. She was handing down laws and judgments to her people, dividing the labor of building fairly or assigning it by lot — when suddenly Aeneas saw, surging up in the middle of a great crowd, Antheus and Sergestus and brave Cloanthus, and others of the Trojans whom the black storm had scattered across the sea and carried off to other shores. He froze, and so did Achates, struck at once with joy and fear. They were burning to clasp the hands of their friends, but the strangeness of it left them uncertain and held them back. So they stayed hidden, watching from the hollow cloud — what had happened to the men? On what shore had they left the fleet? Why had they come? For these were chosen men from every ship, come to plead for mercy, and they made for the temple with a great clamor.

When they had entered and been given leave to speak before the queen, the eldest, Ilioneus, began calmly: "Your majesty — to whom Jupiter has granted the founding of a new city, and the power to bridle proud nations with justice — we are Trojans, wretched, storm-tossed over every sea, and we beg you: keep your people from burning our ships. Spare a god-fearing race; look more closely at what we are. We have not come to put your homes to the sword or to drive off plunder to the shore. That is not the way of the beaten, and we have not the heart for it. There is a country the Greeks called Hesperia, an ancient land, strong in arms and rich in soil. The Oenotrians settled it; now, they say, a later people call it Italy, after a leader of theirs. We were sailing there when a sudden storm rose with the wild surf and scattered us on hidden reefs, blew us all apart, and flung a few of us here onto your shores. What kind of people are you? What country lets such savagery pass for custom? We are barred from the shelter of the very sand; they take up arms against us and forbid us to set foot on the edge of dry land. If you have no respect for men and the weapons of men, then at least fear the gods, who remember the just and the unjust. We had a king, Aeneas — no man more just, none greater in devotion, none mightier in war. If fate has spared him, if he still breathes the air and isn't lying yet among the cruel shades, then we have nothing to fear, and you would not regret being the first to do us a kindness. We have cities and fields in Sicily too, and a Trojan, King Acestes. Let us only beach our storm-wracked fleet, cut new planks and oars from your forests, so that — if our king and our friends are restored to us — we may set joyful course for Italy. But if the sea has swallowed you, best father of the Trojans, and there is no hope left for Iulus, let us at least sail back to the straits of Sicily, to the home that is ready for us there, and to King Acestes." So Ilioneus spoke, and all the Trojans murmured their assent.

Dido looked down a moment, then answered briefly: "Trojans, let go of your fear; put your worries aside. Hard times and the newness of my kingdom force me to such caution, to set a guard over all my borders. Who hasn't heard of the race of Aeneas, of the city of Troy and its courage and its men, of the great fire of that war? We Carthaginians are not so dull-witted as all that; the sun does not yoke his horses so far from our city. Whether you choose great Hesperia and the fields of Saturn, or the country of Eryx and King Acestes — I'll send you off safely, with help and supplies. Or would you like to settle here with me, as equals, in this kingdom? The city I am building is yours. Beach your ships. Trojan and Tyrian, I will treat you all the same. And I only wish your king himself, Aeneas, had been driven here by the same wind! In fact I'll send trusted men along the whole coast and order them to search every corner of Libya, in case he's been shipwrecked and is wandering in some forest or town."

These words stirred the spirits of brave Aeneas and faithful Achates, and for a while now they had been longing to break out of the cloud. Achates spoke first: "Son of the goddess — what are you thinking now? You can see for yourself that everything is safe: the fleet recovered, the friends restored. Only one is missing, and we saw him go down in the waves with our own eyes. Everything else matches what your mother told you." He had barely finished when the cloud around them suddenly tore open and melted into clear air.

Aeneas stood there in the open daylight, shining, his face and shoulders like a god's — for his mother herself had breathed beauty into his hair, the rose-glow of youth into his face, and a glad light into his eyes, the way a craftsman's hand gives grace to ivory, or sets silver and Parian marble in gold. Then, to the queen, and to everyone's astonishment, he spoke at once: "Here I am — the man you are looking for. Aeneas of Troy, snatched from the Libyan waves. You alone have taken pity on Troy's unspeakable suffering. You offer to share your city and your home with us — the leavings of the Greek war, worn down by every disaster on land and sea, stripped of everything. To thank you as you deserve is beyond us, Dido — beyond any of us, beyond the whole scattered Trojan race. If the gods have any care for the good, if justice means anything anywhere, if a clear conscience counts for something, may the gods reward you as you deserve. What lucky age brought you into the world? What great parents gave the world a daughter like you? As long as rivers run to the sea, as long as shadows move across the slopes of the mountains, as long as the sky feeds the stars, your honor and your name and your praise will live on, wherever I am called." With that he reached out his right hand to his friend Ilioneus, and his left to Serestus, and then to the others in turn — to brave Gyas, to brave Cloanthus.

Dido stood transfixed, first at the sight of the man himself, then at all he had endured. "Son of a goddess," she said, "what fate hunts you through such dangers? What force has thrown you onto these wild shores? Are you really the Aeneas whom kindly Venus bore to Anchises of Troy, by the waters of the Phrygian Simois?

I remember — I was only a child — when Teucer came to Sidon, an exile from his homeland, looking to my father Belus for a new kingdom; and Belus was sacking rich Cyprus at the time and holding it under his conquering hand. From that day I have known the story of the fall of Troy, and your name, and the kings of Greece. Even Troy's enemy used to praise the Trojans, and liked to trace his own line back to the old kings of Troy. So come in, young heroes, into my house. I too was driven through long hardship and tossed from place to place before fate let me settle at last in this land. Having suffered myself, I have learned to help those in trouble." With that she led Aeneas into the royal palace, and at the same time ordered sacrifices in the temples of the gods. And she did not forget his men down on the shore: she sent them twenty bulls, a hundred bristling boars, a hundred fat lambs with their mothers, and the glad gift of wine. Inside, the palace was being laid out for a feast of royal splendor: tapestries worked with proud purple were spread, the tables loaded with massive silver, and figures of Dido's ancestors chased in gold — the whole long line of a great people, traced back through the years from its first founder.

Aeneas, his father's love for the boy not letting his heart rest, quickly sent Achates ahead to the ships to carry the news to Ascanius and bring him back to the city — Ascanius was all his anxious thought — and to fetch gifts rescued from the ruins of Troy: a mantle stiff with gold-embroidered figures, and a veil bordered with yellow acanthus, that had once belonged to Argive Helen — her mother Leda's gift, that she had carried from Mycenae when she sailed to Troy and her forbidden marriage. There was a scepter, too, that Priam's eldest daughter Ilione had once carried, and a string of pearls, and a double crown of jewels and gold. Achates hurried off toward the ships to do all this.

But Venus was turning new schemes over in her heart, laying new plans. She would have Cupid take on the look and shape of sweet Ascanius, come in his place, and slip his fire into the queen with the gifts, kindling a flame in her very bones. For Venus mistrusted that two-faced house, those treacherous Tyrians; cruel Juno galled her, and her worry came back as night fell. So she spoke to her winged son: "My boy — you are my strength, my whole power; my son, you who laugh at the great Father's thunderbolts — I come to you for help, and beg your power, like a suppliant. You know how your brother Aeneas is driven over every sea, all around the coasts, by Juno's relentless hate, and you have grieved with me over it many times. Now Phoenician Dido has him, and is holding him with soft words; and I'm afraid where Juno's hospitality will lead. She won't sit still at such a turning of fate. So I mean to outrun her — to take the queen by surprise and ring her round with flame, so that no power can change her, and she's mine, bound fast with a great love for Aeneas. Now hear how I think you can do it. The boy Ascanius — my dearest care — is getting ready, at his father's call, to go up to the Carthaginian city with gifts saved from the sea and the fire of Troy. I'll lull him into a deep sleep and hide him away on the heights of Cythera, or in my shrine at Idalium, so that he can't find out the trick or stumble into the middle of it. You take on his shape — it's only for one night, no more — and, a boy yourself, slip into the boy's familiar face, so that when Dido takes you into her lap in the joy of the feast, among the royal tables and the flowing wine, when she hugs you and kisses you, you can breathe a hidden fire into her and pour your poison through her unknowing veins." Cupid obeyed his dear mother, took off his wings, and walked along, delighted, in Iulus's shape.

Venus, meanwhile, poured a gentle sleep over Ascanius and gathered him warm into her arms, carried him up to the high groves of Idalium, where soft marjoram breathed its sweet shade and fresh flowers folded around him. And now Cupid, obedient, was on his way with the royal gifts for the Carthaginians, glad to follow Achates. When he arrived, the queen had already settled on a golden couch beneath splendid hangings and taken her place in the center; and now Aeneas and the Trojan youth came in and reclined on the spread purple. Servants poured water over their hands, brought out bread from baskets, and handed round smooth napkins. Inside, fifty serving girls were lined up to keep the long tables stocked and to feed the household fire; a hundred more, and as many young men their equals in age, loaded the tables with food and set out the cups. The Carthaginians too came crowding in through the festive halls and took their places on the embroidered couches. They marveled at Aeneas's gifts, marveled at Iulus — at the god's glowing face and his counterfeit words — at the mantle and the veil bright with its yellow acanthus border. Above all, the poor queen, already doomed, with her eye on the coming ruin, could not look her fill: she was moved as much by the boy as by the gifts. He, when he had hung on Aeneas in a long embrace and satisfied the love of the father who thought he was his son, went to the queen. Dido clung to him with her eyes and her whole heart, holding him close, never guessing what a mighty god was settling against her, poor woman. But he, remembering his Cyprian mother, began little by little to wipe out Sychaeus, and tried to take a heart long quiet, long out of practice in love, by surprise with a living passion.

When the first lull came in the feast and the tables were cleared, they set out the great mixing-bowls and crowned the wine with garlands. The hall filled with noise; voices rolled through the wide rooms. Lamps hung blazing from the gilded ceiling, and the torches beat back the night. Then the queen called for the heavy golden bowl, thick with jewels, that Belus and all his line after him had used, and filled it with unmixed wine. The hall fell silent, and she spoke: "Jupiter — since they say you give strangers their rights — grant that this be a day of joy for the Tyrians and for these travelers out of Troy, a day our children will remember. Let Bacchus, giver of gladness, be with us, and bountiful Juno; and you, Carthaginians, keep this gathering with goodwill." She tipped the first drops of wine onto the table as an offering, then touched the bowl lightly to her lips and passed it to Bitias with a challenge. He drank deep, draining the brimming gold, and after him the other lords. Then long-haired Iopas, taught by mighty Atlas, struck up on his golden lyre and sang of the wandering moon and the laboring sun; where the human race and the animals came from, and the rain and the fire; of Arcturus, and the rainy Hyades, and the two Bears; why the winter suns hurry so fast to dip into the sea, and what holds back the lingering nights. The Carthaginians roared their applause again and again, and the Trojans took it up. And the doomed queen drew out the night with all kinds of talk, drinking down a long draught of love. She asked endless questions about Priam, about Hector; about the armor the son of the Dawn had worn to Troy; about Diomedes's horses, and how huge Achilles really was. "No — start from the very beginning, my guest," she said at last. "Tell me the whole story: the trap the Greeks laid, the fall of your people, your own long wanderings. For this is the seventh summer now that has carried you, a wanderer, over every land and sea."

paragraphs: They all fell silent and turned their faces toward him, intent. And from his high couch Aeneas, the father of his people, began:

"The grief you ask me to bring back to life, my queen, is beyond words — how the Greeks tore down the wealth of Troy, that kingdom worth weeping over. I saw the worst of it myself; I was a part of much of it. Who could tell such a story — a soldier of the Myrmidons, a man of Dolopian blood, even one of hard Ulysses's own — and keep from crying? And now the dewy night is sliding down the sky, and the setting stars are calling us to sleep. But if you long so much to learn what happened to us, to hear the last agony of Troy in a few words — though my mind shudders at the memory and recoils from the grief — I'll begin.

Beaten in the war, turned back year after year by fate, the Greek commanders built a horse as huge as a mountain, with the craft of Pallas Athena guiding the work, and ribbed its flanks with planks of fir. They gave it out as an offering for their safe return home — that was the story that went around. But deep in its dark sides they sealed a chosen body of men, picked by lot, and packed the great hollow belly of the beast tight with soldiers and weapons.

Off our coast lies Tenedos, an island famous and rich while Priam's kingdom stood — now just a bay where ships can find poor anchorage. The Greeks sailed there and hid themselves along its empty shore. We thought they were gone — gone with the wind, bound for Mycenae. So all of Troy threw off the long years of grief. The gates swung open. What joy it was to walk out and see the Greek camp deserted, the shore abandoned, the empty ground where their army had stood. Here the company of Achilles had pitched; here Ulysses; here the fleet had been drawn up; here the lines had clashed. Some of us stood gaping at the deadly gift to the virgin Minerva, marveling at the sheer size of the horse.

Thymoetes was the first to urge that it be hauled inside the walls and set in the citadel — whether he was a traitor, or whether the fate of Troy was already bending that way, I cannot say. But Capys, and those with sounder heads, told us to throw this trap of the Greeks, this gift we should never trust, into the sea — or burn it — or bore into the belly and search out whatever was hidden there. The crowd split, pulled both ways, and could not decide.

Then Laocoön came running down from the heights of the citadel, a great crowd streaming after him, and while he was still far off he shouted: "You poor fools! What madness is this? Do you really believe the enemy has sailed away? Do you think any gift of the Greeks comes without a trap? Is this what Ulysses is known for? Either there are men shut up inside this wood, or it's an engine built against our walls, made to look down into our homes and come down on the city from above — there's some trick in it, some lie. Trojans, do not trust this horse. Whatever it is, I fear the Greeks even when they come bearing gifts."

With that he put all his strength into a great spear and hurled it at the beast's curved flank, where the belly joins the frame. It struck and stood there quivering, and the whole hollow chamber groaned and gave back a deep boom from the wound. If the gods had not been against us, if our own minds had not been blind, he would have driven us to hack open that Greek hiding place with our blades — and Troy would be standing still, and you, high tower of Priam, would still be standing.

But then — look — some Trojan herdsmen came dragging a young man toward the king, hands bound behind him, all of them shouting at once. He was a stranger who had thrown himself in their way on purpose, to bring this very thing about, to open Troy to the Greeks. He was sure of his nerve, and ready for it either way: to pull off the trick, or to die. From every side the young men of Troy came pouring up to see the prisoner, crowding around, jeering at him. Now hear how the Greeks set their trap, and learn from this one man's treachery what the whole nation was capable of.

He stood there in the middle of all those eyes, helpless, unarmed, looking around at the ranks of Trojans, and said: "Where on earth, where on any sea, is there a place left for me now? What's left for me, in the end, with nowhere to turn — no home among the Greeks anymore, and the Trojans furious, screaming for my blood?" That cry turned our feeling. The anger died down. We pressed him to tell us where he came from, what he had to say, what we might trust in a captured enemy. At last he set his fear aside and spoke:

"Whatever happens to me, my king, I'll tell you the whole truth. I won't deny that I'm a Greek — that first of all. Fortune has made Sinon wretched, but she will never make him a liar. Maybe some rumor of the name Palamedes has reached your ears — a famous man, of glorious renown, whom the Greeks put to death on a lying charge of treason, on perjured evidence, just because he spoke against the war. Now that he's dead they mourn him. My father, who was poor, sent me as a boy to fight in this war as Palamedes's companion, for we were kin. As long as he stood firm in power, with weight in the councils of the kings, I too had a name, I too had some honor. But when he fell — through the spite of that schemer Ulysses (you all know the story) — I dragged out my life in the shadows, in grief and rage at the ruin of an innocent man. And I did not keep quiet. I swore that if I ever made it home to Argos, I would have my revenge — and with those words I made a deadly enemy.

That was the first crack in my ruin. From then on Ulysses kept terrifying me with new accusations, kept dropping dark hints among the men, kept looking for a way to destroy me. He never rested until, with Calchas as his tool — but why am I telling you this bitter, useless story? Why hold you up? If all you Greeks are the same to you, and it's enough that I'm one of them, then punish me now. That's what the man of Ithaca wants; the sons of Atreus would pay well for it." Now of course we were burning to know more, to hear the rest — with no idea what we were dealing with, no notion of Greek cunning on this scale. Trembling, he went on, and every word was a lie:

"Many times the Greeks longed to give up, to abandon Troy and sail home, worn out by the endless war — and how I wish they had! But again and again the wild winter sea shut them in, or a gale rose and frightened them out of going. And once the horse was finished, framed from maple beams, the storms thundered across the whole sky. Baffled and afraid, we sent Eurypylus to ask Apollo's oracle what to do, and he came back from the shrine with a grim answer: 'With blood you bought your first crossing to Troy, Greeks — with a girl's life sacrificed. With blood you must buy your return; the price is a Greek soul.' When that ran through the ranks, every man went cold; a shudder went down to the bone. Whose death were the Fates demanding? Whom did Apollo want?

Now the man of Ithaca made his move. He dragged Calchas the prophet out into the middle of the crowd and demanded to know what the gods were asking. Plenty of men already saw where this cruel trick was aimed, and watched in silence as it came for me. For ten days Calchas held his tongue, refusing to name anyone, to send a man to his death by a word. But at last, hounded by Ulysses, he broke — as the two of them had arranged all along — and named me as the sacrifice. Everyone agreed. Each man, terrified for himself, was glad to see the doom fall on one poor head instead. The dreadful day came. The salted meal was made ready, the ribbons were tied around my brow. But I broke free, I admit it. I snapped my bonds and ran, and hid all night in the mud of a reedy marsh, waiting for them to set sail — if they ever would. And now I have no hope of ever seeing my old home again, my sweet children, the father I long for. The Greeks will make them pay for my escape, poor souls, with their own deaths. So I beg you — by the gods above who know the truth, by whatever honest faith is left anywhere among men — pity a suffering past all deserving. Pity a man who has done you no wrong."

We spared his life for those tears — and more than that, we pitied him. Priam himself was the first to order the chains and tight cords struck off the man, and he spoke to him gently: "Whoever you are, forget the Greeks you've lost from now on. You're one of us. But answer me straight: why did they build this monstrous horse? Whose idea was it? What's it for — worship, or war?" He answered, schooled in all the tricks and treachery of the Greeks, lifting his freed hands to the stars: "You everlasting fires of heaven, you powers no man may violate, I call you to witness — and you, the altars and the cruel blades I fled, the ribbons I wore as a victim: it is right for me now to break the sacred bond I owed the Greeks, right to hate those men and drag every secret of theirs into the light. No law of my own country holds me now. Only you, Troy — keep your promise, and keep faith with me, if what I tell you saves you and is the truth.

Every hope the Greeks had, all their confidence in this war, rested from the start on the help of Pallas Athena. But from the moment that godless pair — Diomedes and Ulysses, the great inventor of crimes — dared to tear her fateful image, the Palladium, from her holy temple, cut down the guards on the citadel heights, and lay their bloody hands on the sacred statue, defiling the virgin's sacred bands — from that moment the tide of Greek fortune slipped backward and began to ebb. Their strength was broken; the goddess turned her face away. And she gave no doubtful sign of it. The image was barely set down in the camp when flame flashed from its staring eyes, salt sweat ran down its limbs, and three times — a marvel to tell — it leaped from the ground of its own accord, shield and spear quivering. At once Calchas declared they must take to the sea and flee — that Troy could never be taken by Greek weapons unless they went back to Argos for fresh omens, and brought the goddess's blessing home again across the water, the way they had carried it out in their curved ships. And now they have sailed for home, for Mycenae, to gather their strength and the gods on their side, and they'll come back across the sea before you expect them. That is what Calchas reads in the signs.

Warned by him, they built this image to make up for the wounded Palladium, to atone for the outrage to the goddess. And Calchas told them to raise it this huge, this mountain of timber, on purpose — so it could never be brought through your gates or inside your walls, never shelter your people under the old protection. For if your hands defiled Minerva's gift, then utter ruin would fall on Priam's kingdom and the Trojans — may the gods turn that omen back on Calchas instead! But if your own hands brought it up into your city, then Asia would march all the way to the walls of Mycenae in a great war, and that doom would fall on our children."

So, by such treachery and the cunning of one lying Sinon, the thing was believed. We were trapped by tricks and forced tears — we, whom neither Diomedes nor Achilles of Larissa, nor ten years of war, nor a thousand ships had ever broken.

Then something more terrible, far more frightening, struck our blind hearts. Laocoön, the priest chosen by lot to serve Neptune that year, was sacrificing a great bull at the altar — when two serpents came gliding over the calm sea from Tenedos in enormous coils (I shudder to tell it) and made for the shore side by side. Their breasts reared up among the waves; their blood-red crests rose above the water; the rest of them skimmed the sea behind, their huge backs winding in coil after coil. The water roared and foamed. Now they were on the land, their burning eyes streaked with blood and fire, their tongues flickering and licking their hissing mouths. We scattered, white with fear. But the serpents drove straight at Laocoön. First they seized his two small sons, one in each set of coils, and wrapped around them, and tore at their little limbs with their fangs. Then they took the father himself, who came running to help with his spear in hand, and bound him in their huge loops — twice around his waist, twice around his neck, their scaly backs towering over him. And all the while he was straining at the knots with his hands, his priestly ribbons soaked with gore and black venom, sending up screams to the sky like the bellowing of a wounded bull that has shaken the axe from its neck and fled the altar. Then the two serpents slid away to the heights of the citadel, to cruel Minerva's shrine, and coiled at the goddess's feet, sheltered under the curve of her shield.

At that, a fresh terror crept into every shaking heart. People said Laocoön had paid for his crime, as he deserved — he had wounded the sacred wood with his spear, hurled his cursed weapon into its back. "Bring the image to her temple!" they cried. "Pray to the goddess to forgive us!" So we broke open our own walls and laid the city's defenses bare. Everyone set to work. They fitted rollers under the horse's feet and looped ropes of hemp around its neck, and the deadly thing climbed the wall, pregnant with armed men. Around it boys and unmarried girls sang hymns and reached up, thrilled, to lay a hand on the rope. On it came, gliding into the heart of the city, looming over us. O my country! O Troy, home of the gods, walls of the sons of Dardanus famous in war! Four times it stopped on the very threshold of the gate, and four times the weapons inside it clashed. Yet we pushed on, blind, out of our minds, and set the cursed thing in our holy citadel. And even then Cassandra opened her mouth and foretold the doom to come — but by the will of a god the Trojans never believed her. Poor fools, on what would prove our last day we hung the shrines of the gods with festive boughs all through the city.

Meanwhile the sky wheeled around and night came rushing up out of the sea, wrapping the earth and the heavens and the tricks of the Greeks in its great shadow. Through the town the Trojans lay still, their tired bodies held by sleep. And now the Greek fleet was sailing back in formation from Tenedos through the friendly quiet of the moon, making for the shore it knew so well — when the royal galley raised the signal fire. And Sinon, kept safe by the cruel will of the gods, slipped open the wooden bolts and let the Greeks out of the belly of the horse. It swung wide and gave them back to the air, and out they came, glad of it: the captains Thessandrus and Sthenelus, and deadly Ulysses, sliding down a rope they'd lowered; Acamas and Thoas, Neoptolemus of the line of Peleus, the prince Machaon first of all, and Menelaus, and Epeos himself, the man who had built the trap. They poured into a city drowned in sleep and wine. They cut down the few sentries, threw the gates wide open to welcome in their comrades, and joined the two halves of the army together.

It was the hour when sleep first comes to weary men, the kindest gift of the gods, stealing over them — when in my dream, there before my eyes, Hector appeared, deep in grief, weeping rivers of tears. He was as he had been when the chariot dragged him, black with bloody dust, his swollen feet pierced through with the thongs. God, the sight of him — how changed he was from the Hector who once came home wearing the armor stripped off Achilles, or who flung Trojan fire onto the Greek ships. His beard was matted, his hair caked with blood, and across his body were all the wounds he took fighting for the walls of his home. Weeping myself, I seemed to speak to him first, and I forced out these words of grief: "Light of Troy, surest hope of the Trojans — what kept you so long? What shore do you come from, Hector, the one we longed for? After so many of your own men have died, after so much suffering by your people and your city, how worn we are to see you at last. But what has done this shameful thing to your clear face? Why do I see these wounds?"

He said nothing, wasted no time on my empty questions, but groaned heavily from the depths of his heart and said: "Run, son of the goddess — get yourself out of these flames. The enemy holds the walls. Troy is falling from her height. You've given enough to your country and to Priam. If any hand could have saved Troy, mine would have saved it. Troy entrusts her holy things to you now, and her household gods. Take them with you to share your fate; find them the great city you will build at last, when you have wandered the whole sea." With that he carried out in his hands the sacred ribbons, the power of Vesta, and the everlasting fire from the inner shrine.

Meanwhile the city was sinking into chaos and grief, and though my father Anchises's house stood apart, set back among trees, the noise grew clearer and clearer and the horror of war closed in. I shook off sleep and climbed to the roof, to the highest point, and stood there straining to listen. It was like a fire driven by a furious wind into a field of grain, or a mountain torrent in flood, flattening the crops and the labor of the oxen, dragging whole forests down headlong — while some shepherd, knowing nothing, hears the roar from a cliff and stands there stunned. Then the truth was plain; the Greeks' treachery lay open. Already the great house of Deiphobus had crashed down in flame, with the fire god towering over it; already his neighbor Ucalegon was burning. The wide straits of Sigeum threw back the glare. The shouting of men rose up, and the blare of trumpets. Out of my mind, I grabbed my weapons — though there was no plan in fighting, only the wild urge to gather a band of men and rush the citadel. Rage and fury drove me headlong, and I thought how fine it is to die fighting.

Then Panthus, Apollo's priest at the citadel, escaped the Greek blades and came stumbling to my door, dragging his little grandson by the hand and carrying the holy things, the conquered gods of Troy. "Where is the worst of it, Panthus?" I cried. "What stronghold can we hold?" He barely finished groaning before he answered: "It's come — the last day, the hour Troy cannot escape. We Trojans are no more; Ilium is no more; the great glory of our people is gone. Jupiter has handed it all to Argos. The Greeks are masters of a burning city. The horse stands high in the middle of the town, pouring out armed men, and Sinon, the winner now, mocks us as he spreads the fire. Thousands are streaming through the wide-open gates, as many as ever came from great Mycenae. Others block the narrow streets with leveled spears. A line of naked steel stands ready, flashing, for the kill. The watchmen at the gates barely put up a fight, blindly, in the dark."

His words, and the will of the gods, drove me into the fire and the fighting, wherever the grim Fury called, wherever the roar and the cries that rose to heaven called me. Rhipeus joined me, and Epytus, a great fighter, in the moonlight; Hypanis and Dymas fell in at my side, and young Coroebus, son of Mygdon — he had come to Troy in those last days, on fire with mad love for Cassandra, bringing his men to help Priam, his father-in-law to be. Poor man — he never listened to the warnings his prophetess bride gave him. When I saw them packed together and willing to fight, I said: "Men — bravest of hearts, but it's no use — if you're set on following a man who'll go to the end, you see how it stands with us. Every god who held this empire up has left his altar and his shrine. The city you're defending is already in flames. So let's die — let's throw ourselves into the thick of it. The one safety for the beaten is to hope for none." That put a wild fury into their hearts.

Then, like wolves running blind in a black fog, driven by the cruel hunger in their bellies while their cubs wait dry-mouthed back in the den, we went out through enemy spears toward certain death, straight down the middle of the city, with the dark night around us in its hollow shadow. Who could put into words the ruin of that night, the slaughter? Who has tears enough to match the suffering? An ancient city was falling, after all those years of power. Bodies lay everywhere through the streets, in the houses, on the sacred steps of the gods. And it was not only Trojans who paid in blood — sometimes the courage came back into the beaten, and the winning Greeks went down. Everywhere there was grief, everywhere terror, and death in a thousand shapes.

Androgeos was the first of the Greeks to cross our path, a big troop of his men with him. He took us for friends, fellow soldiers, and called out carelessly: "Hurry up, men! What's kept you so slow? The others are sacking and burning Troy already — are you only now coming up from the ships?" Then — because no answer of ours rang true — he knew at once he'd fallen among enemies. He froze, choked on his words, and shrank back. Like a man who steps hard on a snake hidden in rough ground and recoils in horror as it rears up in fury, swelling its blue-black neck — that's how Androgeos shuddered and tried to run. We charged, ringed them with our blades, and cut them down where they stood, panicked, lost, with no idea of the ground. Fortune smiled on our first stroke.

Coroebus, flushed with the win and his own daring, called out: "Friends — Fortune has shown us the safe road, the road that's on our side. Let's take it. Let's change shields and put on Greek emblems. Trick or courage — who asks which against an enemy? They'll arm us themselves." With that he put on Androgeos's plumed helmet and his fine emblazoned shield, and buckled the Greek sword at his side. Rhipeus did the same, and Dymas, and all the men, gladly, arming themselves from the fresh kill. We moved out mingled with the Greeks, fighting under gods not our own, and in the blind dark we clashed with them again and again and sent many of them down to the underworld. Some scattered to the ships and ran for the safety of the shore; some, in their shameful fear, scrambled back up into the horse and hid in its familiar belly.

But you can put no trust in anything when the gods are against you. Just then Cassandra, the daughter of Priam, was being dragged by her loose hair out of the temple, out of the very sanctuary of Minerva, lifting her burning eyes to heaven in vain — her eyes, for her tender hands were bound. Coroebus could not bear the sight. Mad with grief, he threw himself into the middle of them, ready to die, and we all charged after him into the thick of the fight. And here the first blow fell on us — from the high roof of the temple our own people buried us under a hail of weapons, taking us for Greeks by the false crests we wore. Then the Greeks, roaring with rage at the rescue of the girl, gathered from every side and fell on us — Ajax most fierce of all, the two sons of Atreus, the whole army of the Greeks. It was like the moment when storm-winds break loose and clash, the West, the South, and the East riding high on his horses of dawn; the forests scream, and Nereus rages with his trident and churns the sea up from its floor. And those Greeks we'd scattered in the dark and chased through the city came back too — they were the first to spot our shields and lying weapons, and to mark how strange our speech sounded. In a moment we were crushed by sheer numbers. Coroebus fell first, killed by Peneleus at the altar of the warrior goddess. Then Rhipeus went down — the most honest man, the most just, in all of Troy. The gods saw it otherwise. Hypanis and Dymas died run through by their own friends. And you, Panthus, when you fell, neither your great goodness nor Apollo's holy band could shield you. Ashes of Troy, last flames that took my people — be my witnesses that on that night I never flinched from any Greek spear, from any risk, and that if the Fates had wanted me dead, I earned it by my own hand.

We were torn away from there — myself, and Iphitus, slowed by age, and Pelias, hobbling from a wound Ulysses had given him. New shouting called us toward Priam's palace. There the fighting was so wild it was as if no one were dying anywhere else in the whole city, as if this were the only war on earth. We saw the Greeks storming the place, locking shields over their heads in a tortoise-shell to push up to the very threshold. Ladders clung to the walls; men climbed the doorposts toward the door itself, holding their shields up with the left hand against the spears, gripping the eaves with the right. The Trojans on top tore down the towers and the whole roof of the palace and hurled the pieces, using these for weapons now that the end was on them — gilded beams, the splendor of the old kings. Below, men with drawn swords packed the doorway and held it. We threw ourselves back into it, to help the palace, to put fresh fight into the beaten men.

There was a hidden door at the back, a secret passage running through the rooms of Priam's house, a postern that linked the buildings. While the kingdom stood, poor Andromache used to come and go that way alone, bringing little Astyanax to his grandfather. I climbed through it up to the highest ridge of the roof, where the helpless Trojans were flinging weapons that came to nothing. A tower rose there at the very edge, lifting its top into the sky — all of Troy could be seen from it, the Greek ships, the whole camp. We attacked it with iron where the high floors had loosened the joints, wrenched it out of its bed, and heaved it over. It crashed down with a roar and broke apart across a wide stretch of the Greek ranks, crushing them. But more kept coming, and the stones and every kind of missile never let up.

Out in front of the entrance hall, on the very threshold, Pyrrhus was raging, glittering in the bright bronze of his armor — like a snake fed on poisonous plants that has lain swollen underground all winter and now, sloughed and shining, fresh and new, rears its breast to the sun and flickers its forked tongue. With him came huge Periphas, and Automedon, Achilles's old charioteer, and all the young men of Scyros, hurling fire up onto the roof.
