Pyrrhus himself, out front, took an axe and split the hard doorposts and tore the bronze-plated doors from their hinges. He cut a beam clean through, gouged a great window in the solid oak, and threw the inner house open to view: the long halls came into sight, the private rooms of Priam and the old kings, and the armed enemy standing on the threshold.

Inside, the house was one long cry of grief and confusion. The vaulted rooms rang with the wailing of women; the sound struck the golden stars. Terrified mothers wandered the great halls, clinging to the doorposts, pressing their lips to them. Pyrrhus came on with all his father's force; no bolt, no guard could hold him. The doors gave way under the battering ram and crashed off their hinges. Force broke a road through. The Greeks poured in, butchered the first men they met, and filled the whole place with soldiers. No flood is so wild when it bursts its banks and overwhelms the dikes and pours raging across the fields, sweeping cattle and barns away over the whole plain. I saw it with my own eyes — Pyrrhus drunk on slaughter in the doorway, and the two sons of Atreus; I saw Hecuba and her hundred daughters and daughters-in-law, and Priam at the altars, fouling with his blood the fires he had himself made holy.

Maybe you'll ask how Priam died. When he saw his captured city fallen, the doors of his palace torn open, the enemy in the heart of his home, the old man pulled his long-unused armor over shoulders shaking with age — useless. He buckled on his useless sword and went to meet the enemy, looking for his death. In the middle of the courtyard, under the open sky, stood a great altar, and beside it an ancient laurel that leaned over it and held the household gods in its shade. There Hecuba and her daughters had crowded together at the altar for nothing — like doves driven down by a black storm — clinging to the images of the gods. But when she saw Priam in the armor of his young manhood, she cried out: "What dreadful thought, my poor husband, made you put on these weapons? Where are you running? This is no time for that kind of help, not even if my Hector himself were here. Come here to me. This altar will protect us all, or we'll die together." And she drew the old man to her and made him sit by the holy place.

Just then Polites, one of Priam's sons, came running, having slipped through the swords of the Greeks, down the long colonnades, across the empty courtyards, wounded. Pyrrhus was after him, hot for the kill, almost on him, reaching for him with the spear — until Polites came out into the open before his parents' eyes and fell, and poured out his life in a flood of blood. Then Priam, though death already had him by the throat, could not hold back. He cried out in rage: "For this crime, for what you have dared, may the gods — if there is any justice in heaven that cares about such things — pay you what you deserve. You have made a father watch his own son die; you have fouled a father's eyes with murder. The man you lie about being your father, the great Achilles, was never like this to his enemy Priam. He respected a suppliant's claim, an enemy's trust. He gave me back the bloodless body of Hector for burial and sent me home to my own kingdom." With that the old man threw a spear, but feebly, with no force behind it; it rang harmlessly off the bronze and hung dangling from the boss of the shield.

Pyrrhus answered: "Then you can take this news to my father, the son of Peleus, in person. Remember to tell him about his grim son Neoptolemus, and all my ugly deeds. Now — die." And as he said it he dragged the old man, trembling and slipping in his own son's blood, right up to the altar; he wound his left hand in Priam's hair, and with his right lifted the flashing sword and buried it to the hilt in his side. So ended Priam. This was the death the Fates gave him — to see Troy in flames and her towers fallen, the man who had once ruled so many lands and peoples, the great lord of Asia. Now he lies a huge trunk on the shore, the head torn from the shoulders, a corpse without a name.

Then, for the first time, raw horror closed around me. I stood frozen. The image of my own dear father rose up before me as I watched a king of the same great age gasp out his life from that brutal wound. I thought of Creusa, left alone, of my plundered house, of the fate of little Iulus. I looked back to see what men I still had, but every one of them had given out, exhausted, and thrown himself down to the ground or into the fire.

So I was alone — and then I saw, sitting silent in the sanctuary of Vesta, hiding herself in a corner, the daughter of Tyndareus, Helen. The bright fires lit her up as I wandered, my eyes everywhere. She was afraid of the Trojans, who hated her for the fallen city, afraid of the Greeks' revenge and the rage of the husband she'd abandoned — Helen, the curse of Troy and her own homeland alike. There she crouched, a thing accursed, clinging to the altar. A fire blazed up in my heart: a fury to avenge my dying country, to make her pay for her crimes. "So she'll sail home to Sparta and Mycenae unharmed? She'll walk in like a queen, in triumph? She'll see her husband again, her home, her parents and her children, with a train of Trojan women and slaves to wait on her — while Priam lies butchered, while Troy burns, while our shore has soaked up our blood again and again? Never. There's no glory in punishing a woman — that fight wins no honor — but people will praise me for stamping out something evil, for making the guilty pay what they owe. And it will be sweet to fill my soul with the flame of revenge and satisfy the ashes of my people." These were the wild thoughts pouring through me —

when my gracious mother appeared, never so clear to my eyes before, shining pure light through the dark, showing herself as a goddess, as tall and lovely as the gods above her know her. She caught me by the hand to hold me back, and these were the words from her rose-bright lips: "My son — what bitterness has stirred up this ungovernable rage? Why this fury? Where has your care for me gone? Shouldn't you look first to where you left your father, worn out with age — to whether your wife Creusa is still alive, and the boy Ascanius? Greek lines are roving all around them, and if my care for them weren't standing guard, the flames would have taken them by now, and the enemy's sword would have drunk their blood. It is not the hated face of the Spartan woman, not Paris, that you should blame — it is the gods, the merciless gods, who are tearing down all this wealth and toppling Troy from her height. Look — I'll strip away the cloud that hangs over your mortal sight and blunts it, the damp veil around you. Don't be afraid of any order your mother gives you; don't refuse to obey. There — where you see the great blocks ripped apart, stone torn from stone, the smoke and dust boiling up — Neptune is shaking the walls and the foundations loose with his huge trident, prying the whole city up from its bed. There Juno, the cruelest of all, holds the Scaean gates, sword at her side, raging, calling up the allied army from the ships. Look back — Pallas Athena has taken the high citadel, blazing out of the storm-cloud with her Gorgon shield. The Father himself feeds the Greeks their courage and rouses the gods against the weapons of Troy. Run, my son. Make an end of this struggle. I will never leave your side; I'll set you safe at your father's door."

She finished and vanished into the thick of the night. And now the dread shapes came clear to me, the great powers that hate Troy. Then I saw the whole of Ilium sinking into the flames, all of Neptune's Troy uprooted from the ground — like an ancient ash tree high in the mountains that farmers race to bring down, hacking at it turn after turn with iron and the axe. It threatens and threatens, its head shaking, its high branches trembling, until little by little the wounds win and it gives one last groan and tears away from the ridge and comes down in ruin. I climbed down, and with the goddess leading me I made my way through the flames and the enemy. The weapons drew back; the fires gave way.

But when I reached the door of my home, my father's old house, the one man I wanted most to carry first to safety up in the high hills — my father Anchises — refused to live on once Troy was gone, refused to go into exile. "You who still have the warm blood of youth in you," he said, "and the strength to stand on your own — you run. As for me, if the gods above had wanted me to live, they would have spared my home. It's enough, more than enough, that I've already seen one sack of this city and lived through it. Say your goodbye to my body and leave it lying here. I'll find my own death. The enemy will pity me, or want my armor. Losing a grave is nothing. For too long I've dragged out a life the gods hate, useless, ever since the father of gods and men breathed his lightning over me and touched me with his fire."

He kept saying it, fixed in his resolve. We were all in tears — myself, my wife Creusa, Ascanius, the whole household — begging the old man not to drag everything down with him, not to lean his weight on the doom that was already crushing us. He refused, clinging to his place and his decision. Again I felt the pull of the weapons, longing for death in my misery — for what plan, what hope was left? "Did you really think I could take a step and leave you here, Father? Could a thing so monstrous fall from a father's lips? If it's the will of heaven that nothing of this great city be left, if you're set on it — set on throwing yourself and all of us into Troy's grave — the door to that death stands wide open. Pyrrhus will be here any moment, fresh from Priam's blood, the man who butchers the son before the father's eyes and then the father at the altar. Was it for this, dear mother, that you carried me through the fire and the spears — to see the enemy inside my house, to see Ascanius, and my father, and Creusa beside them, slaughtered in each other's blood? Weapons, men, bring me my weapons — the last light is calling the beaten. Send me back to the Greeks. Let me see the fight again. We will not all die today unavenged."

I was buckling on my sword again, working my left arm into the shield, on my way out of the house — when there in the doorway my wife Creusa threw herself down, clinging to my feet, holding little Iulus up to his father. "If you're going out to die, take us with you, whatever comes. But if you've learned anything from fighting, and you put any hope in these weapons, then guard this house first. Who are you leaving little Iulus to, and your father, and me, who used to be called your wife?" Her cries filled the whole house — when out of nowhere a sudden wonder appeared. There between our hands, between the faces of his grieving parents, a soft tongue of flame seemed to pour light from the top of Iulus's head, a fire that did him no harm, licking at his soft hair and feeding around his brow. Frightened, we shook the burning hair and tried to put out the holy fire with water. But my father Anchises lifted his eyes to the stars in joy and raised his hands and his voice to heaven: "Almighty Jupiter — if any prayer can move you, look down on us; that's all I ask. And if our faithfulness has earned it, give us a sign, Father, and confirm this one."

The old man had barely spoken when a sudden crack of thunder broke on the left, and a star shot down through the dark sky trailing a torch of light. We watched it glide high over the roof and bury its brightness in the forest of Mount Ida, marking out our road. It left a long furrow of light behind, and all around the place reeked of sulfur. At that, my father rose, won over at last. He spoke to the gods and worshiped the holy star: "Now, now there's no more delay. I'll follow, gods of my fathers — wherever you lead, I am with you. Save my house, save my grandson. This sign is yours; Troy is in your keeping still. I give in, my son. I won't refuse to go with you."

He finished — and by now the fire was louder across the city, rolling its tide of flame closer. "Then come, dear father, climb up onto my neck. I'll carry you on my own shoulders; the weight won't trouble me. However it turns out, the danger and the safety will be the same for both of us. Little Iulus will come along beside me, and my wife will follow our steps at a distance. And you, my servants, listen. Just outside the city there's a mound with an old temple of Ceres on it, abandoned now, and an ancient cypress beside it that our fathers kept holy for many years. We'll all meet there, coming by different ways. You, Father, carry the sacred things, our country's gods, in your hands; I've just come from the fighting and the slaughter, and it would be a sin for me to touch them until I've washed in running water."

With that I bent down and spread a lion's skin over my neck and broad shoulders and took up my burden. Little Iulus laced his fingers in mine and trotted to keep up with his father's longer stride, and behind us came my wife. We went on through the shadows. And I — who a moment before had faced flying spears and the whole massed army of the Greeks without flinching — now took fright at every breath of wind, startled at every sound, terrified for the boy at my side and the father on my back. I had nearly reached the gates, and thought I'd come safely through it all, when suddenly there seemed to be a great thudding of feet close by, and my father, peering into the dark, cried out: "Run, my son, run — they're coming. I can see the glow of their shields, the flash of the bronze." Here some cruel power — I don't know what — robbed me of my wits in my fear. For while I hurried down side streets, off the road I knew, my wife Creusa — was she stopped by some grim fate, did she lose her way, did she sink down exhausted? I will never know. She was gone, and I never saw her again. I didn't look back, didn't even think of her, until we reached the mound and the old shrine of Ceres. There, when we all gathered at last, she alone was missing — lost to her husband, her son, her friends.

Out of my mind, I blamed every man and god there is. In all the wreck of the city I saw nothing crueler than this. I left Ascanius, my father, and the gods of Troy in my friends' care, hidden in a winding valley, and went back into the city, strapping on my shining armor again. I was set on hunting through all of Troy once more, on throwing my life back into the danger. First I made for the walls and the dark gate I'd come out by, and traced my own steps backward through the night, searching the way with my eyes. Everywhere was horror; the very silence struck terror into me. Then I went to my house, in case — just in case — she'd found her way back there. The Greeks had broken in and filled the whole place. The hungry fire was rolling up to the rooftop on the wind; the flames towered over it, raging into the air. I pushed on to Priam's palace and the citadel. In the empty colonnades of Juno's sanctuary, the chosen guards Phoenix and grim Ulysses were keeping watch over the loot — the treasure of Troy hauled out of the burning shrines, the altars of the gods, the golden bowls and the stolen robes, all heaped together. Children and frightened mothers stood around it in a long line. I even dared to throw my cries into the dark. I filled the streets with my grief, calling Creusa over and over, hopelessly, again and again.

As I went searching, raging endlessly through the houses of the city, there rose before my eyes the sorrowful ghost of Creusa herself — her very shape, but larger than the woman I had known. I froze; my hair stood on end and my voice stuck in my throat. Then she spoke, to ease the grief out of me: "Why give yourself up to this wild sorrow, my sweet husband? None of this happens without the will of the gods. It is not allowed for you to take Creusa with you from here — the great ruler of high Olympus does not allow it. Long exile is yours, a vast plain of sea to plow, and then you'll come to the land of Hesperia, where the Lydian Tiber flows gently through the rich farmland of brave men. There happiness is waiting for you, and a kingdom, and a royal bride. Dry your tears for the Creusa you loved. I will never see the proud homes of the Greeks, or go to be a slave to some Greek wife — I, a daughter of the line of Dardanus, the daughter-in-law of the goddess Venus. No: the great mother of the gods is keeping me here, on this soil. Now goodbye, and keep your love for the son we share." When she had said this, she left me weeping, with so much I wanted to say, and faded into thin air. Three times I tried to throw my arms around her neck; three times the ghost I grasped at slipped through my hands like a light wind, like a dream that takes wing.

And so, the night spent at last, I came back to my friends. There I found, to my astonishment, that a great crowd of new arrivals had gathered — mothers and men, young people come together for exile, a sad host. They had streamed in from every side, ready in heart and goods to follow me across the sea to whatever land I chose. And now the morning star was rising over the high ridges of Mount Ida, bringing the day. The Greeks held the gates, blocked tight; there was no hope of help. I gave it up, lifted my father onto my back, and made for the mountains."
books.title: The Fall of Troy

books.label: Book III
paragraphs: When the gods had brought down the kingdom of Troy and Priam's throne — undeserving as it was — when proud Ilium had fallen and all of Neptune's Troy lay smoking on the ground, the omens of heaven drove us out to seek some far-off, empty land for a home. So below Antandros, at the foot of Mount Ida, we built a fleet, with no idea yet where the Fates would let us settle or where we were allowed to stop. We gathered our men. Spring had barely begun — the first warmth, my father Anchises giving the word to trust ourselves to fate and the sea. And weeping, I left the shores of my country, the harbor, the plains where Troy had been. I went out onto the deep an exile, with my comrades and my son, with my household gods and the great gods of our people.

Far off lay a wide land of war, the country of the Thracians, with broad plowed fields, once ruled by fierce Lycurgus — an old friend to Troy, our gods joined to theirs, as long as our luck held. I sailed there, and on that curving shore I laid out the walls of a first city, though fate was already against me, and I called it Aeneadae, after my own name. I was making offerings to my mother Venus and to the gods who bless a new beginning, and killing a sleek white bull on the altar to the high king of heaven. Close by there happened to be a mound, crowned with a thicket of cornel and bristling myrtle. I went up to it and tried to tear some green branches from the ground, to roof the altar in leaves — and I saw a thing horrible to tell, beyond belief. From the first bush I pulled up, the roots tore loose and drops of black blood oozed from them and stained the earth. A cold shudder went through me; my blood froze with terror. Still I tried again, pulling at the stubborn stem of a second, to find out what was hidden underneath — and from the second too the blood ran dark.

I turned it over in my mind, full of dread, and prayed to the nymphs of those fields and to Father Mars, who watches over the land of Thrace, asking them to make the sign harmless and lift the curse. But when I set my knees against the ground and strained at a third shoot, harder still — I can hardly say it — a groan came up out of the depths of the mound, and a voice reached my ears: "Aeneas, why do you tear at me? I am buried here — spare me. Don't stain your faithful hands. I am no stranger to you: I was born in Troy, and this blood you see is not running from a tree. Flee this cruel country, get away from this greedy shore. I am Polydorus. An iron harvest of spears pinned me down here, and out of them this thicket of sharp shafts has grown."

Then I stood dumb, my mind crushed under the weight of fear, my hair standing up, my voice locked in my throat. This Polydorus — long ago, when Troy was already failing, old Priam had sent him in secret to the king of Thrace to be raised, loaded with a great weight of gold, because Priam had given up hope in the Trojan cause and was sick at heart watching the city under siege. And the Thracian, when Troy's power broke and her fortune left her, went over to the winning side, to Agamemnon. He shattered every law of decency; he murdered Polydorus and seized the gold. There is nothing the cursed hunger for gold will not drive men to do. When the fear had drained out of me, I brought the omens of the gods before our leaders, my father first, and asked them what they thought. They were of one mind: leave this poisoned land, this place where the bond of a host had been so foully broken, and let the south wind carry the fleet away. So first we held a funeral for Polydorus. We heaped fresh earth high over the mound and raised altars to his ghost, dark with mourning bands and black cypress; the Trojan women stood around with their hair loose in the way of grief. We poured out bowls of warm milk and dishes of holy blood, laid the soul to rest in its tomb, and called out his name one last time.

Then, as soon as we could trust the sea, when the winds had quieted the waves and a soft southerly was calling us to the deep, my men hauled the ships down to the water and crowded the shore. We left the harbor; the lands and cities slid away behind us.

There is an island worshiped in the middle of the sea, dear to the mother of the sea-nymphs and to Neptune of the Aegean. Once it drifted from coast to coast, until the dutiful Archer-god, Apollo, chained it fast between two of its sisters, Myconos and Gyaros, and gave it a stillness it could keep — a place that laughs at the winds. There the sea carried us, and there the calm waters offered our weary ships a safe harbor at last. We came ashore and bowed to Apollo's city.

Anius, who was both king of the people and priest of Apollo, came out to meet us, his brow bound with the sacred fillets and the laurel of the god. He knew my father at once, an old friend, and we joined hands and went into his house. I went to the god's temple, built of ancient stone, and prayed: "God of Thymbra, give us a home of our own. Give a tired people walls, a line of descendants, a city that will last. Keep alive this second Troy, this remnant the Greeks and merciless Achilles left us. Whom should we follow? Where do you send us? Where do you tell us to settle? Father, give us a sign, and come down into our hearts." I had barely finished when everything seemed to shake at once — the doorway and the laurel of the god, the whole mountain heaving, the tripod groaning as the inner shrine swung open. We dropped to the ground in awe, and a voice came: "Hard-enduring sons of Dardanus, the land that first bore your fathers' line will take you back again to her glad breast. Go, search out your ancient mother. There the house of Aeneas will rule over all the world's shores, and his children's children, and the children born to them." So Apollo spoke, and a great wave of joy broke loose with our shouting, and everyone asked: what city is this? Where is the god sending us, telling us to come home?

Then my father, turning over in his mind the old stories of our people, said: "Listen, leaders of Troy, and learn where your hope lies. There is an island in the middle of the sea, Crete, the island of great Jupiter, where another Mount Ida stands — the cradle of our race. Men live in a hundred great cities there, the richest of kingdoms. From there, if I remember the tale right, our first father Teucer sailed to the Trojan shore and chose the site of his kingdom, before Ilium had walls or the towers of Troy stood; from there came our way of life, and the worship of the Mother of the gods of Mount Cybele, and the bronze cymbals of her rites, and the grove sacred to her, and the lions yoked beneath her chariot. So come — let us follow where the gods lead. Let us calm the winds with sacrifice and make for the harbors of Crete. It is no long voyage: if Jupiter is with us, the third dawn will set our fleet on the Cretan shore." With that he laid the proper offerings on the altars — a bull to Neptune, a bull to you, beautiful Apollo, a black sheep to the storm-god and a white one to the kindly west winds.

A rumor flew that King Idomeneus had been driven out of his father's kingdom of Crete and gone into exile, so the coast lay empty, the houses abandoned, a home standing ready for us. We left the harbor of Delos and flew over the open water, past Naxos with its wine-dark ridges where the worshipers of Bacchus dance, past green Donusa, Olearos, snow-white Paros, and the Cyclades scattered across the sea, threading the crowded channels among the islands. The sailors' cries rose as they bent to the work, and they urged each other on — "For Crete! For our fathers' country!" A following wind sprang up astern and drove us, and at last we came in to the ancient shores of Crete. There, eager, I laid out the walls of the city I had longed for and named it Pergamea, after the citadel of Troy, and I told my people, glad to hear it, to love their new home and raise a fortress over it. The ships were already drawn up on the dry sand; the young men were busy with marriages and new-plowed fields, and I was handing down laws and houses — when out of a rotten quarter of the sky a wasting sickness fell on us, a plague on our bodies and on the trees and the crops, a whole season of death. Men gave up their sweet lives, or dragged themselves along sick; the Dog Star scorched the fields barren, the grass withered, the blighted harvest gave us no food. My father told me to go back across the sea to Delos and Apollo's oracle, to beg the god for mercy: where would he set an end to our suffering, where did he tell us to turn for help, which way should we steer?

It was night, and sleep had taken hold of every living thing on earth. The sacred images of my gods, the household gods of Troy — the Penates — that I had carried out of the burning city through the flames, stood before me as I lay there — clear and bright in the full light of the moon as it poured through the windows. And they spoke to me, and lifted the weight off my heart: "What Apollo would tell you if you sailed all the way to Delos, he tells you here instead, and sends us to your door to say it. We followed you out of Troy when it burned, with you we crossed the swelling sea in your ships, and we will lift your children yet unborn up to the stars and give your city power over the world. Build great walls for great men. Don't give up the long road, the labor of wandering. You must change your home. This is not the coast Apollo of Delos meant for you; he never told you to settle on Crete. There is a country the Greeks call Hesperia, an old land, strong in war and rich in soil; the Oenotrians lived there, but now, men say, a later people have named it Italy, after their leader. That is our true home. There Dardanus was born, and Father Iasius, the first root of our race. Get up. Go gladly to your old father and tell him there is no mistaking it now: he must look for Italy. Jupiter forbids you the fields of Crete."

I was stunned by the vision and the voices of the gods — for this was no dream; I seemed to know their faces there in front of me, the sacred bands in their hair, their living features. A cold sweat broke out all over me. I sprang up from the bed and lifted my hands to heaven with my prayers and poured an offering of unmixed wine on the hearth-fire. Glad to have made the rite, I went to Anchises and laid the whole thing out for him in order. He saw the truth of it at once — that our line came from two stocks, two ancestors, and that he had been deceived by the old confusion of names. He said: "My son, you whom the fate of Troy has driven so hard — Cassandra alone foretold all this to me. I remember now how she kept naming Hesperia for our people, kept naming the kingdoms of Italy. But who then believed a Trojan would ever reach the shores of Hesperia? And who paid any attention to Cassandra's prophecies? Let us give way to Apollo, and take the better road he shows us." So he spoke, and we all obeyed him gladly.

We left that place too, leaving a few of our people behind, and spread our sails and ran before the wind over the wide and empty sea. When the ships had reached deep water, with no land left in sight anywhere — only sky on every side and sea on every side — a black storm-cloud massed over my head, bringing night and foul weather, and the waves shuddered in the dark. At once the winds churned the sea and threw up huge swells; we were scattered far apart across the heaving water. Clouds smothered the day, and the wet night blotted out the sky; lightning split the clouds again and again. We were knocked off our course and wandered blind across the deep. Even Palinurus, our helmsman, swore he could not tell day from night in the sky and had lost the way in the middle of the sea. For three whole days, as far as we could judge in the blind dark, we drifted on the water, and for three nights without a star. On the fourth day at last we saw land begin to rise — distant hills, and threads of smoke going up. We dropped the sails and bent to the oars, and the sailors whipped the blue water into foam.

The shore that took me, saved from the waves, was the Strophades — "the Turning Islands," the Greeks call them — set in the great Ionian Sea, the dreaded home of Celaeno and the other Harpies, ever since they were shut out of Phineus's house and fled in fear from the tables they used to foul. No fouler monster than these, no crueler plague, no curse of the gods, ever rose from the waters of the underworld. They have the faces of girls and the bellies of filthy birds; their hands are hooked claws; their faces are always pale with a hunger nothing can fill.

When we put in there, we saw fat herds of cattle scattered across the fields and flocks of goats grazing the grass with no one tending them. We fell on them with our swords, and called the gods and Jupiter himself to take a share of the spoils. Then we built up couches on the curving beach and feasted on the rich meat. But all at once, swooping down from the mountains with a horrible beating of wings, the Harpies came, and tore at the food, and fouled everything they touched with their filthy claws, and left a sickening stench behind in the screaming. So we moved off, deep under a hollow rock walled in by trees and trembling shadows, and laid the tables again and lit the altar fires fresh. And again, out of another quarter of the sky, out of their hidden roosts, the screeching pack came down on the prey with their hooked claws and slimed our meal with their mouths. Then I told my men: arm yourselves, we will make war on this foul brood. They did as I said. They hid their swords in the grass and laid their shields out of sight, and when the Harpies came swooping along the curving shore with their loud wings, Misenus from a high lookout sounded the charge on his bronze horn. My men attacked — a strange kind of battle, to gash these filthy sea-birds with the sword. But no blow could pierce their feathers or wound their backs; they shot up into the sky and left the prey half-eaten and the foul tracks behind them.

Only one stayed, Celaeno, perched high on a crag, a prophetess of doom, and these words burst from her: "Sons of Laomedon — first you slaughter our cattle, now you are ready to make war on us and drive us, who have done nothing wrong, out of our own country? Then take these words of mine and fix them in your hearts. What the all-powerful Father foretold to Apollo, and Apollo to me, I, the eldest of the Furies, now reveal to you. Italy is the land you are steering for; you call on the winds, and to Italy you will go, and you will be allowed into her harbors. But you will not wall in the city you have been promised until a terrible hunger and the wrong you have done us drive you to gnaw and devour your very tables." She finished, and beat her wings and fled back into the forest. The blood froze in my men; their courage broke; they wanted no more war, but begged me to ask the gods' pardon with prayers and offerings — whether these things were goddesses or only foul and monstrous birds. And my father Anchises, on the shore, stretched out his open hands and called on the great gods and named the offerings owed them: "Gods, turn this threat aside! Gods, keep this curse from falling! Be kind, and save a people who keep faith with you." Then he told us to wrench the cables from the shore and let out the sails. The south wind stretched the canvas, and we ran over the foaming water wherever the wind and the helmsman carried us.

Now the wooded island of Zacynthos rose from the waves, and Dulichium, and Same, and Neritos with its sheer cliffs. We steered clear of the reefs of Ithaca, the kingdom of Laertes, and cursed the land that bred cruel Ulysses. Soon the cloud-wrapped peak of Leucata came into view, and Apollo's headland that sailors dread. Worn out, we made for it and put in to the little town. We dropped anchor from the prows and beached the sterns. And so, having reached dry land at last, beyond all hope, we cleansed ourselves before Jupiter and burned our offerings on his altars, and held games on the shore of Actium in the old Trojan way. My men stripped, slick with oil, and wrestled in the contests of home — glad to have slipped past so many Greek cities and held our course through the heart of enemy country. Meanwhile the sun rolled through the full circle of the year, and icy winter roughened the sea with its north winds. I nailed up on the temple doors a shield of hollow bronze that great Abas had once carried, and marked the gift with a line of verse: AENEAS DEDICATES THESE ARMS, TAKEN FROM THE CONQUERING GREEKS. Then I gave the order to leave the harbor and man the oars. My men struck the sea and swept it white, and quickly we lost sight of the heights of Phaeacia, skirted the coast of Epirus, and ran into the harbor of Chaonia, up to the high city of Buthrotum.

There an unbelievable rumor reached us: that Helenus, a son of Priam, was ruling Greek cities, that he had taken the throne and the wife of Pyrrhus, son of Achilles, and that Andromache had passed once more to a husband of her own people. I was astonished, and my heart burned to speak to the man and learn the strange story. So I left the ships in the harbor and walked up from the shore. As it happened, I found Andromache in a grove outside the city, by the waters of a stream they called by the name of Simois, pouring out the yearly offerings, the sad gifts to the dead, at an empty tomb of green turf she had raised to Hector, with two altars, a place where she could weep. When she saw me coming, and saw Trojan arms around me, she went out of her mind with terror at the impossible sight, and stiffened in the middle of staring at me, the warmth going out of her body. She nearly fell, and only after a long silence did she find her voice: "Is it really you, alive — a true face, a true messenger, son of the goddess? Are you living? Or if the kind light has left you, then where is my Hector?" She said it, and broke into tears, and filled the whole grove with her crying. There was little I could say to her grief; shaken, I managed only a few broken words: "I am alive — alive through every kind of misery. Don't doubt it; what you see is real. What has become of you, fallen so far from such a husband? Or has any fortune kind enough found you again, worthy of you — Hector's Andromache, still wife to Pyrrhus?"

She lowered her eyes and answered in a low voice: "Happiest of all was Priam's daughter Polyxena, ordered to die on an enemy's tomb, under the high walls of Troy — who never had to draw lots for a master, never had to lie a captive in the bed of a conqueror. We, our city burned, were carried over far seas, and I bore the arrogance of Achilles' son, that boy in his pride, and gave him a child in slavery. Then he chased after Hermione, Helen's daughter, a marriage among Spartans, and handed me, his slave, to Helenus, his slave, to keep. But Orestes, on fire for the bride that had been stolen from him, and driven mad by the Furies for his own crimes, caught Pyrrhus off his guard and cut him down at his father's altar. When Pyrrhus died, part of his kingdom passed to Helenus, who named these plains Chaonia, and this whole country Chaonia, after Chaon of Troy, and built a Pergamum, a Trojan citadel, on the ridge. But you — what winds, what fates set you on this course? What god drove you, not knowing it, onto our shores? And the boy Ascanius — does he live? Does he still breathe the air? Born to you while Troy still stood... Does the boy grieve at all for the mother he lost? Do his father Aeneas and his uncle Hector fire him toward the old Trojan courage, the old manhood?" She poured all this out weeping, raising long sobs that came to nothing, when Helenus, the hero, son of Priam, came down from the city walls with a great company.

He knew his own people, and led us joyfully up to his gates, weeping freely as he spoke at every word. As I walked I recognized a little Troy, a copy of the great citadel, and a dry streambed they called Xanthus, and I threw my arms around the posts of a Scaean Gate. The other Trojans, too, took their pleasure in the friendly city. The king received them in his wide colonnades; in the middle of the hall they poured offerings of wine and held the cups while the feast was set on gold. Day followed day, and the breezes called us to the sails; the south wind bellied out the canvas. So I went to the prophet-king and put my questions to him: "Son of Troy, voice of the gods — you who know the will of Apollo, the tripod, the laurel of the god, the stars and the language of the birds and the omens of their flight — tell me. Every sign has promised me a fortunate voyage; all the gods have urged me by their will to make for Italy and try those distant shores. Only Celaeno the Harpy sings a strange new horror, an unspeakable curse, and threatens a black famine. What dangers should I shun first? What must I do to ride out so much hardship?"

Helenus first sacrificed the bullocks in the proper way and begged the gods' favor; then he loosed the bands from his holy head and led me by the hand to the threshold of Apollo's temple, my mind trembling at the nearness of the god, and from his prophet's mouth he sang: "Son of the goddess — for it is beyond all doubt that you sail the deep under the high blessing of heaven; the king of the gods deals out the fates this way and rolls the wheel of fortune so — I will tell you a few things out of many, so you can cross the strange seas more safely and find a berth at last in an Italian harbor. The rest the Fates forbid Helenus to know, and Juno will not let me speak. First, the Italy you think so near, whose ports you mean to make as if they were close at hand — a long, trackless distance of sea keeps it far off and shuts it away from you. You must bend your oars in the waters off Sicily, and cross the salt plain of the Italian sea, and pass the lakes of the underworld and the island of Circe before you can build your city on safe ground. I will give you the signs; hold them in your heart. When you are anxious, and you find by the waters of a hidden river, under the oaks along its bank, a great white sow stretched on the ground with a litter of thirty white piglets around her teats — that is the place for your city, that is the sure rest from your labors. And don't shrink from the threat of gnawing your tables; the Fates will find a way, and Apollo will be there when you call him.

"But these nearer shores of Italy, the coast washed by our own sea — keep away from them; every town is held by hostile Greeks. The Locrians of Naryx have walled a city there; Idomeneus has filled the Sallentine plains with his soldiers; there stands the little fortress of Petelia, raised by Philoctetes of Meliboea, trusting its walls. And when your fleet has crossed and lies anchored, and you raise the altars to pay your vows on the shore — veil your hair with a purple cloth, so that in the worship of the gods no hostile face can cross your sight and break the omens. Keep this way of covering the head, you and your men; let your children's children hold to it as a sacred rule.

"When you leave that place, and the wind carries you up to the coast of Sicily, and the narrows of Pelorus open out — steer for the land on your left, and the long sea on your left, and keep wide of the shore and the waters on your right. These two, men say, were once one country, until an age long ago tore them apart with a vast convulsion — time can work such change — and the sea rushed in with force between them and cut Italy off from Sicily, and now a narrow channel washes the towns and fields along both sundered coasts. On the right side waits Scylla; on the left, merciless Charybdis, who three times a day sucks the whole sea sheer down into the pit of her whirlpool and three times spews it back up to lash the stars. But Scylla hides in a blind cave, and thrusts out her mouths to drag ships onto the rocks. From the waist up she has the look of a girl, a fair-breasted woman; below, she is a sea-monster of huge size, a body of wolves and dolphins joined to a belly of howling dogs. Far better to lose time and go the long way around Cape Pachynus, swinging wide, than to catch one glimpse of misshapen Scylla in her vast cave, or hear the rocks ring with her sea-blue hounds.

"And one thing more — if Helenus has any foresight, if a prophet is to be trusted, if Apollo fills his heart with truth — one thing above all I will tell you, son of the goddess, and tell you again and again: pray to great Juno first; pray to her with all your heart. Win the powerful queen over with willing vows and gifts, and bend her to you with prayers. Only so, with Sicily behind you, will you be sent across to the borders of Italy. And once you are landed there, when you come to the town of Cumae, to the haunted lakes and the rustling forest of Avernus, you will find a prophetess in her frenzy, deep in a cave below the rock, who chants the fates and writes their words and names on leaves. Whatever verses she writes on the leaves she sets in order and shuts away in her cave; they lie still and keep their place. But if the door swings open and the smallest breath of wind stirs them, scattering the tender leaves through the hollow rock, she never tries to catch them again as they fly, never puts the verses back in order; her visitors go away with no answer, cursing the Sibyl's cave.

"No matter how your men grudge you the delay, no matter how loudly the voyage calls and the fair wind fills your sails — beg the prophetess to chant the fates aloud, in her own voice, and to unseal her lips and speak. She will tell you the peoples of Italy, the wars to come, and how to flee each hardship or bear it, and if you honor her she will grant you a safe passage. This is all I am allowed to warn you of. Go now, and lift the greatness of Troy to the stars by all you do."

When the prophet had said this in his kindness, he had heavy gifts of gold and carved ivory carried down to my ships, and stowed great weights of silver in the holds — cauldrons of Dodona, a coat of mail triple-woven with hooks of gold, and a splendid helmet with a flowing crest of horsehair, the armor of Pyrrhus himself. He had gifts for my father too. He found us horses and guides, filled out the crews, and fitted my comrades with arms.

Meanwhile Anchises was telling us to rig the sails and not waste the favoring wind. And the prophet of Apollo spoke to him with great respect: "Anchises — you whom Venus thought worthy of her proud love, twice cared for by the gods, twice saved from the wreck of Troy — there before you lies the land of Italy; sail for it. And yet you must coast far past this nearer part of it; the Italy Apollo opens to you is far away. Go on, blessed in the love your son bears you. Why do I say more, and hold you back while the south wind rises?" Andromache, too, sad at this last parting, brought robes worked with figures of gold and a Trojan cloak for Ascanius, and would not be outdone in kindness; she loaded him with gifts of woven cloth and said: "Take these as well, my child — keepsakes made by my own hands, tokens of Hector's Andromache and her lasting love. Take the last gifts of your own people, you who are all that is left to me now of my Astyanax. He had your eyes, your hands, your face; he would be growing up beside you now, a boy your own age."

As I turned to go, the tears welled up, and I said: "Live happily, you whose fortune is already made and behind you. We are called from one fate into another. For you, peace is won; you have no sea to plow, no ever-retreating fields of Italy to chase. You look on an image of the river Xanthus, on a Troy your own hands built — under a better star, I pray, and out of the path of the Greeks. If I ever reach the Tiber and the fields along its banks, if I ever see the walls granted to my people, then someday we will make our two cities, our two kindred nations, one in spirit — Hesperia and Epirus, both sprung from Dardanus, both broken by the same fate — one Troy in two hearts. Let our children keep that bond forever."

We sailed on, past the Ceraunian heights, where the crossing to Italy is shortest by sea. Meanwhile the sun went down and the hills lay dark in shadow. We drew lots for the oars and stretched out on the lap of the welcome land at the water's edge, and slept along the dry shore, our bodies eased with rest. Night, driven by the Hours, had not yet climbed to her height when Palinurus, never one to sleep on watch, got up to read the winds and listen for every breath of air, marking all the stars sliding through the silent sky — Arcturus, the rainy Hyades, the two Bears, and Orion in his golden armor. When he saw the whole sky calm and settled, he gave the clear signal from the stern; we broke camp, set out, and spread the wings of our sails.

And now, as Dawn reddened and put the stars to flight, we saw far off the dim blue hills and the low line of Italy. Achates was the first to call out "Italy!" and my men shouted "Italy!" with a roar of joy. Then my father Anchises wreathed a great bowl with garlands, filled it with unmixed wine, and standing high on the stern called the gods: "You gods who rule the sea and the land and the storms, give us an easy run with the wind, and breathe kindly on us!" The wind freshened as he prayed; the harbor opened nearer, and a temple of Minerva came into view on the heights. My men furled the sails and swung the prows toward shore. The harbor is curved like a bow against the eastern surge, with two jutting reefs that foam with spray and hide the haven within; the temple drew back and seemed to flee inland behind its sheltering rocks. There the first omen I saw was four horses, white as snow, grazing the wide grass. And my father Anchises said: "War — that is what you bring us, land of strangers; horses are armed for war, and these herds threaten war. Yet these same beasts can be broken to the chariot and made to take the bit and pull in harness, side by side; so there is hope of peace as well." Then we prayed to the holy power of Pallas Athena, who first welcomed us with the sound of her name, and we veiled our heads before the altar with Trojan cloths, and following Helenus's strict command we burned the proper offerings to Argive Juno. Without delay, the moment our vows were paid, we turned the tips of our sail-clad yards out to sea and left those shores, that ground we could not trust, the homes of Greeks.

From there we sighted the bay of Tarentum, the city of Hercules, if the story is true, and across from it the temple of the Lacinian goddess rose, and the towers of Caulon, and Scylaceum, the wrecker of ships. Then, far off across the waves, Mount Etna came into view, and we heard the great groan of the sea hammering the rocks, the broken voices on the shore, the surge leaping in the shallows and the swell churned up thick with sand. My father Anchises cried: "This must be the Charybdis the prophet warned of — these are the rocks, the terrible reefs Helenus foretold! Pull away, men, all together — lay on the oars!" They did as he said. Palinurus was the first to throw the groaning prow to port and out to sea, and the whole fleet bent that way under oar and wind. The swell heaved us up to the sky on its curling back, then the trough sank away beneath us down to the underworld. Three times the cliffs roared in their hollow caves; three times we saw the spray burst and run down dripping from the stars. Meanwhile the wind dropped and the sun set, and worn out, not knowing the way, we drifted in to the shore of the Cyclopes.

The harbor itself is wide and untroubled by any wind, but close beside it Etna thunders in ruin. Now it heaves a black cloud up to the sky, a tower of pitch-dark smoke shot through with glowing ash, and throws up balls of fire that lick at the stars; now it spews out boulders, the very entrails torn from the mountain, and groaning, hurls molten rock into the air, and boils up from its deepest pit. The story is that the giant Enceladus, his body half-burned by Jupiter's bolt, lies pinned under all that mass, with mighty Etna piled on top of him breathing flame through its burst vents; and as often as he rolls his weary side, the whole of Sicily shudders and groans and a pall of smoke veils the sky. All that night we hid in the woods, enduring the monstrous terrors, with no way of seeing what made the noise. For there was no fire of the stars, no clear vault lit by the constellations; the sky was thick with cloud, and the dead of night held the moon shut behind it.

The next day was just breaking, the first sun chasing the wet mist from the sky, when out of the woods, suddenly, a strange shape of a man came toward us, worn to nothing, in pitiful rags, his hands stretched out to the shore in supplication. We stared. He was filthy past belief, his beard wild, his clothes pinned together with thorns — but a Greek for all that, one of those who had once sailed against Troy in the war. When he saw the Trojan dress and the Trojan arms in the distance, he froze a moment at the sight, then broke and rushed down to the shore in tears and prayers: "By the stars, I beg you, by the gods above, by this clear air we all breathe — take me away, Trojans, carry me off to any land at all, and that will be enough. I admit I am one of the Greeks who sailed against Troy; I admit I made war on your gods. For that, if my crime is so great, scatter me piece by piece across the waves, drown me in the wide sea — I would rather die, if die I must, at the hands of men." He had thrown himself at our knees and clung there, groveling. We pressed him to say who he was, of what blood, and what fortune had hunted him here. My father Anchises, after only a moment, gave the young man his hand and steadied his courage with the plain pledge of it. At last, his fear set aside, he told us his story:

"I am from Ithaca, a comrade of luckless Ulysses, and my name is Achaemenides. My father was Adamastus, a poor man — and I wish to god I had stayed poor at home. I sailed for Troy, and here my shipmates left me behind, forgotten in the huge cave of the Cyclops as they bolted in terror from that cruel door. It is a house of gore and bloody feasts, vast and dark inside. The monster himself is so tall he strikes the high stars — gods, take such a plague off the earth! — no man can bear to look at him or speak to him. He gorges on the flesh and the black blood of the wretched. I saw it with my own eyes: I saw him snatch up two of our company in his great fist, sprawl back in the middle of his cave, and dash their bodies against the rock until the threshold ran and swam with their blood; I saw him chew the limbs, dripping black gore, the warm joints still quivering under his teeth.

"But Ulysses did not let it pass — he never forgot himself, not even in that. When the Cyclops, gorged on his meal and drowned in wine, let his head loll and lay sprawled and enormous across the cave, snoring, belching up gore and gobbets of flesh soaked in wine in his sleep — we prayed to the great gods, drew lots for our parts, and crowded all together around him and bored out that one huge eye, the single eye sunk under his savage brow, as broad as an Argive shield or the disk of the sun, with a sharpened stake. And so at last we took our joy in revenge for the friends he had killed. But run — run, you poor men; cut your cables and flee! For there are a hundred more Cyclopes, as huge and as horrible as Polyphemus penning his woolly flocks in that cave and milking them, scattered all along this curving coast and roaming the high hills. Three times now the horns of the moon have filled while I have dragged out my life in the woods, among the lairs of wild beasts, watching the monstrous Cyclopes from a rock, shaking at the sound of their feet and their voices, living on the bitter berries and stony cornels the branches give, tearing up roots and grass. I watched the whole horizon, and at last I saw your ships come in. Whatever they are, I gave myself up to them; it is enough to have escaped that unspeakable race. I would rather you take my life by any death you please."

He had hardly finished when we saw the shepherd Polyphemus himself on the height of the mountain, heaving his huge bulk among his flocks and making for the shore he knew — a horror, a shapeless mass, monstrous, his eye put out. A lopped pine guides his hand and steadies his step. His woolly sheep go with him; they are his one comfort, his only solace now. When he reached the water and waded out into the deep, he washed the running blood from the socket of his gouged-out eye, grinding his teeth and groaning, and strode far out into the sea — and even there the waves never wet his towering sides. In terror we ran, taking the deserving stranger who had earned it aboard, and cut the cables in silence, and leaning into the oars we swept the sea. He heard us, and turned to follow the sound of the strokes — but when his groping hand could not reach us and he could not match the Ionian swells in his stride, he let out a roar so vast the sea shook to its depths, and the land of Italy far off was struck with fear, and Etna bellowed back through her winding caves. The whole tribe of the Cyclopes, roused, came pouring down from the woods and the high hills and crowded the harbor — we saw them, the brotherhood of Etna, standing there helpless with their wild eyes, their heads in the clouds, a fearful gathering, like tall oaks or cone-bearing cypresses standing in the high forest of Jupiter or the grove of Diana. Sharp fear drove us to shake out the sheets any way we could and spread our sails to the friendly wind. But Helenus had warned us to hold a course between Scylla and Charybdis, a hair's breadth either way from death; we resolved to turn back. And then a north wind came down from the narrow headland of Pelorus and carried us, and I passed the living rock at the mouth of the Pantagias, the bay of Megara, and low Thapsus. Achaemenides showed us the landmarks, retracing the coast of his wanderings with luckless Ulysses.

There is an island that lies across the mouth of a Sicilian bay, facing wave-beaten Plemyrium; the men of old called it Ortygia. The story goes that Alpheus, a river of Greece, forced a secret channel under the sea all the way to here, and now, Arethusa, he mingles with your Sicilian waters at your spring. As we were told, we worshiped the great powers of the place, and from there I passed the rich marshland of low-lying Helorus. Then we skirted the high rocks and jutting reefs of Pachynus, and Camerina came into view in the distance — the town the fates forbade to be moved — and the Geloan plains, and Gela, that takes its grim name from its river. Then steep Acragas showed its great walls far off, the breeder of brave horses once; and I left palm-rich Selinus behind with a following wind and threaded the shallows of Lilybaeum with their hidden reefs. After that the harbor of Drepanum took me in — a joyless landing. There, after all the storms of the sea had battered me, I lost my father Anchises, the comfort of all my cares and griefs. There, best of fathers, you left me worn out, saved from so many dangers all for nothing. Not Helenus the prophet, for all the horrors he foretold, ever warned me of this grief; not the Harpy Celaeno. This was my last ordeal, the end of the long road. And as I sailed on from there, a god drove me at last onto your shores.
So Aeneas, alone, with everyone listening, told the story of the fated road the gods had set him on, and all his wanderings. And here at last he fell silent, and ended, and went to his rest.
